articles.title: Lenovo ThinkSystem SC755 V5 Puts 96 EPYC 9006 CPUs and 24,000 Cores in a Liquid-Cooled Rack
articles.summary: The SC755 V5 puts two dual-socket nodes on a vertical compute tray that slides into Lenovo’s 13U N1380 Neptune enclosure and blind-mates to power, water, and network with no cabling. Each enclosure takes eight trays, and three enclosures fit a standard 19-inch rack, for 48 nodes, 96 processors, and 192TB of DDR5 across two floor tiles. Direct warm-water cooling lets each node run a pair of EPYC 9006 SP7 processors with up to 256 cores and 600W apiece.
bodyEvidence: Lenovo has introduced two ThinkSystem V5 servers built on AMD’s 6th Gen EPYC 9006 SP7 processors: the SC755 V5, a Neptune liquid-cooled dual-socket node for HPC clusters, and the SR755 V5, an air-cooled single-socket 2U rack server. Announced ahead of SC26, the launch also covers the ThinkSystem DE6500 and DE6800 NVMe block arrays, validation of the Cornelis CN5000 fabric, and new AI factory and colocation services. A full rack of SC755 V5 trays holds 96 processors and more than 24,000 cores.

The SC755 V5 puts two dual-socket nodes on a vertical compute tray that slides into Lenovo’s 13U N1380 Neptune enclosure and blind-mates to power, water, and network with no cabling. Each enclosure takes eight trays, and three enclosures fit a standard 19-inch rack, for 48 nodes, 96 processors, and 192TB of DDR5 across two floor tiles. Direct warm-water cooling lets each node run a pair of EPYC 9006 SP7 processors with up to 256 cores and 600W apiece.

Each node has 16 memory channels per CPU and takes up to 4TB across 32 DIMM slots, with RDIMMs at 8,000MT/s and MRDIMMs at 12,800MT/s supported. It adds two PCIe Gen6 x16 low-profile slots, up to six E3.S SSDs, and two 25GbE ports, and Lenovo lists InfiniBand, Omni-Path, and Ethernet as fabric options. The enclosure integrates up to four 15kW Titanium power conversion stations with N+1 redundancy and accepts inlet water from the dew point up to 45°C, which Lenovo says removes the need for chillers.

Lenovo says the design removes up to 100% of system heat through water and delivers up to 40% higher sustained performance than similar air-cooled systems, figures from internal testing that vary with configuration, workload, and facility water temperature. Dynamic Partitioning lets operators split the two dual-socket nodes on a tray into four single-socket systems and back, for smaller HPC or agentic AI jobs that do not need the full core count. Dell took the other route with the same 600W processors, cooling two of them on air in the 3U PowerEdge R9825 .

“AI and high-performance computing are converging around a simple customer need: the ability to turn increasingly complex workloads into real outcomes,” said Scott Patti, Vice President, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Lenovo. “That means getting more useful performance from every watt, overcoming growing power and cooling constraints, and moving faster from infrastructure deployment to operational AI.”

The SR755 V5 is a 2U rack server with a single EPYC 9006 processor of up to 256 cores and 16 DDR5 slots at one DIMM per channel, for up to 4TB of RDIMM or MRDIMM memory. Storage runs to 16 front E3.S drives, and two hot-swap M.2 boot drives, and expansion to six PCIe Gen6 slots, two OCP 3.0 slots, and two double-width or two single-width GPUs.

Lenovo aims the SR755 V5 at large-scale virtualization, electronic design automation, financial modeling, engineering, and agentic AI infrastructure in data centers that are staying on air. The company argues that one 256-core socket gives lower power consumption and better economics than dual-socket configurations, a claim it bases on internal analysis. Security features include FIPS 140-3 support, NIST SP800-193 platform firmware resiliency, and post-quantum cryptography readiness through the XClarity Controller.

The DE6500 and DE6800 are 2U, dual-controller block arrays with 24 2.5-inch NVMe bays, and SAS expansion shelves take either to a maximum of 7.2PB raw. Lenovo rates the DE6500 at 1.7 million IOPS and up to 41GB/s of sustained throughput, and the DE6800 at 5 million IOPS and up to 110GB/s. The DE6800 offers up to 12 ports of 200Gb NVMe over InfiniBand, RoCE, or TCP, where the DE6500 tops out at eight 100Gb NVMe over RoCE ports.

Lenovo has also validated the Cornelis CN5000 fabric as an interconnect option for AI and HPC clusters. On the services side, it is adding GPU deployment, configuration, and optimization work to its Hybrid AI Factory Services, with multi-node support for Red Hat AI Enterprise and NVIDIA AI Enterprise with Run:ai. New gigafactory services bring NVIDIA Infrastructure Services expertise for deployment and cluster validation on large builds.

For customers short on data center capacity, Lenovo can now arrange colocation in Digital Realty facilities and act as the single point of contact. That includes use of the Digital Realty Innovation Lab to validate infrastructure and workloads, with financing available through Lenovo TruScale Infrastructure as a Service. Lenovo is showing the new systems at SC26 in booth 3023.

articles.title: Cornelis CN5000 Connects 300 Dual-EPYC 9745 Nodes at GWDG as AMD Joint HPC Program Launches
articles.summary: Cornelis says CN5000 is qualified and in production on AMD EPYC 9005 Series platforms, validated on more than 25 platform configurations, and deployed at university, research, government, and industrial sites across North America and Europe. Qualification now extends to AMD Instinct MI350X Series GPUs . The program targets workloads where compute and network have to scale together: computational fluid dynamics, climate and weather, life sciences, physics, materials science, and other double-precision codes.
bodyEvidence: Cornelis and AMD have launched a joint program to design, validate, and deploy HPC and AI-for-science systems that pair AMD EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs with Cornelis networking, sold through the OEMs and system integrators customers already use. The announcement is anchored by a production system: GWDG’s new EMMY P4 supercomputer in Göttingen, Germany, runs approximately 300 dual-socket EPYC 9745 nodes on a Cornelis CN5000 Omni-Path fabric. Cornelis also gave timing for the next generation, with OEM systems pairing its CN6000 with EPYC 9006 expected from Q1 2027.

Cornelis says CN5000 is qualified and in production on AMD EPYC 9005 Series platforms, validated on more than 25 platform configurations, and deployed at university, research, government, and industrial sites across North America and Europe. Qualification now extends to AMD Instinct MI350X Series GPUs . The program targets workloads where compute and network have to scale together: computational fluid dynamics, climate and weather, life sciences, physics, materials science, and other double-precision codes.

At GWDG, EMMY P4 serves NHR@Göttingen, one of nine centers in Germany’s National High Performance Computing Alliance, and supports thousands of research codes across life sciences, physics, quantum computing, AI, and the digital humanities. It adds capacity to an environment that runs approximately 3.5 million HPC jobs a year. Prof. Dr. Julian Kunkel, deputy head of high-performance computing at GWDG, said the EPYC processors and Cornelis fabric give the center the compute density, low latency, and consistent performance to serve that range of codes.

“Every AMD EPYC generation puts more cores in a node, and every one of those cores needs its own path to the network,” said Lisa Spelman, CEO of Cornelis. “When the network can’t keep up, you pay for compute that sits waiting.”

For each engagement, AMD and Cornelis are combining engineering, field, and partner teams from architecture design and benchmarking through acceptance testing and production. Customers buy through their preferred OEM or integrator and can run their codes at the AMD HPC Center of Excellence in Munich before they commit. The companies plan to publish joint reference designs and application performance data for leading ISV software, and to extend the program to each new EPYC and Instinct generation.

Cornelis has published application results for the pairing: on dual EPYC 9755 servers with CN5000, Siemens Simcenter STAR-CCM+ ran 8.99x faster on eight nodes than on one across nine models, a 112% parallel efficiency. Across 132 CONVERGE CFD workloads on Dell PowerEdge R7725 servers with the same processors, CN5000 delivered 20% higher average throughput than NVIDIA NDR InfiniBand at four nodes. Cornelis cites up to 39% higher throughput across the applications it tested. These are Cornelis results, and we did not run or audit them.

CN6000 is the follow-on, an 800G adapter with a PCIe 6.0 x16 host interface that Cornelis is validating with AMD EPYC 9006 Series processors and next-generation Instinct platforms. Cornelis says CN6000 can give every core in a 512-core, dual-socket server a dedicated connection to the network, and it claims 1.6 billion messages per second and 23% lower MPI latency than NVIDIA XDR InfiniBand, figures it describes as internal measurements and projections. A 512-core, two-socket Venice server is the configuration we tested in the Dell PowerEdge R9825 .

The codes this program targets run in double precision, and AMD says its Instinct MI430X is designed for up to 288 TFLOPS of native FP64, a peak theoretical figure. OEM systems pairing CN6000 with EPYC 9006 platforms are expected beginning in Q1 2027. Cornelis will show EPYC platforms with its networking at SC26 in Chicago at booth 1419.

articles.title: Nexsan Unity NV12000 Puts 15.72PB of NVMe Flash in 10U With 122.88TB QLC SSDs
articles.summary: The NV12000 serves block storage over iSCSI and Fibre Channel, file over NFS and SMB, and S3 object storage through NexObject, so one array can back virtual machines, file shares, and object buckets together. Nexsan aims it at AI and HPC datasets, data lakes, analytics, media production, and virtualized environments on VMware, Proxmox, Hyper-V, and Xen, and lists Scale Computing among its supported third-party platforms. It joins the NV4000, NV6000, and NV10000 in the Unity NV-Series.
bodyEvidence: Nexsan has introduced the Unity NV12000, a 2U dual-controller unified storage array that takes 24 122.88TB QLC NVMe SSDs for nearly 3PB of raw flash in the head unit. Four of the company’s new U2F226 NVMe expansion enclosures, at 26 bays each, bring an all-flash system to 15.72PB raw in 10U, which works out to about 1.57PB per rack unit. Nexsan rates the platform at up to 3 million IOPS, and it is available now through the company’s solution providers.

The NV12000 serves block storage over iSCSI and Fibre Channel, file over NFS and SMB, and S3 object storage through NexObject, so one array can back virtual machines, file shares, and object buckets together. Nexsan aims it at AI and HPC datasets, data lakes, analytics, media production, and virtualized environments on VMware, Proxmox, Hyper-V, and Xen, and lists Scale Computing among its supported third-party platforms. It joins the NV4000, NV6000, and NV10000 in the Unity NV-Series.

Unity Immutable Snapshots lock retention settings once they are applied, which Nexsan says helps prevent unauthorized modification or deletion of protected recovery points. NexObject adds S3 object locking, and the platform includes AES-256 encryption, Kerberos-secured NFS, and optional integration with Nexsan’s Assureon archive. Snapshots run to 2,048 per LUN, and replication is asynchronous at the storage pool level. For Veeam backup targets, Nexsan sells the separate VHR-Series hardened repository.

“AI, analytics and modern enterprise applications are creating unprecedented demands on storage capacity, performance and data protection,” said Vincent Phillips, CEO of Nexsan. “The Unity NV12000 addresses these challenges by delivering petabyte-scale, all-flash capacity in an exceptionally compact footprint, alongside the unified data services and immutable protection organizations need to support critical workloads.”

The NV12000 runs Unity OS 7.4, which Nexsan has also made available across the rest of the NV-Series. Licensing is all-inclusive, covering immutable snapshots, S3 object locking, the Cloud Connector for S3 edge caching, multi-factor authentication, inline compression, deduplication, replication, and FASTier caching. Nexsan says the release adds new capabilities but has not listed them. Each controller carries 512GB of DDR5 on what the company describes as an end-to-end PCIe 5.0 architecture.

The 2U U2F226 is the all-flash expansion path, and four of them alongside the head unit reach the 15.72PB NVMe maximum. The 4U U2G478 takes SAS SSDs or 7,200 RPM hard drives up to 26TB, with as many as eight enclosures and 648 drives in 34U. Nexsan lists 19.17PB raw for that configuration with hard drives and 22.1PB with SAS SSDs, and in hybrid systems FASTier uses flash to cache the hard drive tier.

Nexsan has not published usable capacity, throughput, or the test conditions behind the 3 million IOPS rating. The company cites up to 9x data reduction from deduplication, which will depend on the data.

articles.title: AMD EPYC Venice SP7 Review: 256 Cores Per Socket and the Bandwidth to Feed Them
articles.summary: This review focuses on Venice SP7, AMD’s larger data center socket, which supports sixteen memory channels and processors up to 600W. The enterprise-focused Venice SP8 platform and the LPDDR-based Verano, AMD’s answer to NVIDIA Vera , are slated to arrive next year, in 2027. Our test data comes from the 256-core EPYC 9996 in Dell’s PowerEdge R9825 and from AMD’s Nigeria reference platform, which also gave us a look at the 96-core, 5.3GHz EPYC 9686F and at what MRDIMM-12800 memory adds to the same silicon.
bodyEvidence: AMD’s 6th Gen EPYC server CPU family, codenamed Venice, brings Zen 6 and Zen 6c cores to a lineup built to take on every corner of the server market. AMD is pushing core counts and clock speeds higher and giving those cores considerably more bandwidth to work with, through a larger memory subsystem and the move to PCIe Gen6. The breadth of the family gives AMD room to chase maximum compute density while also building parts around the demands of enterprise servers and AI hosts.

This review focuses on Venice SP7, AMD’s larger data center socket, which supports sixteen memory channels and processors up to 600W. The enterprise-focused Venice SP8 platform and the LPDDR-based Verano, AMD’s answer to NVIDIA Vera , are slated to arrive next year, in 2027. Our test data comes from the 256-core EPYC 9996 in Dell’s PowerEdge R9825 and from AMD’s Nigeria reference platform, which also gave us a look at the 96-core, 5.3GHz EPYC 9686F and at what MRDIMM-12800 memory adds to the same silicon.

The SP7 lineup sets the frame for the architecture discussion that follows. The flagship of the Venice lineup is the EPYC 9996 with 256 cores, a 33.3% increase over Turin’s 192-core EPYC 9965 . AMD is making an even larger jump with its high-frequency parts, moving from a maximum of 64 cores with Turin’s 9575F to 96 cores with the 9686F, a 50% increase in core count, and the 9686F also reaches a maximum boost of 5.3GHz. AMD published the full 31-part EPYC 9006 list in October; the SP7 parts we reference in this review are below.

AMD declared the SP7 parts generally available on November 10, with OEM systems shipping and Azure and OCI instances to follow, and its launch claims set the bar our testing checks against. Against 5th Gen EPYC, AMD puts Venice at 2.0x on SPECint 2026, 2.4x on SPECfp 2026, 2.7x on STREAM, 1.4x on HPL, and 1.3x on DGEMM.

Those are AMD’s figures from AMD’s testing, and we cover its IPC claims with the core design below; our STREAM Triad result, shown below, lands at 1.9x the Turin flagship on DDR5-8000 and 3.0x on MRDIMM-12800.

Against NVIDIA Vera, AMD claims 1.2x per core on SPECrate 2026 integer for its 96-core frequency part and 2.2x per platform for the 9996, and at launch it added 3.7x on SPECrate 2017 for a two-socket 9996, a published 5,470 against an AMD estimate of 1,459 for Vera. The per-core figure matches our pinned 7-Zip result, where the 9686F compressed 16% faster than an Olympus core, and the platform figures bracket our suite, where the 9996’s margin over Vera runs from parity on OLTP to up to 5.4x on crypto code. The same published score is 1.68x the 3,260 of a two-socket EPYC 9965.

AMD also describes three operating points for the lineup. A 256-core part at 400W is pitched at bulk agentic hosting, where utilization runs 50% to 100% and power works out to 1.2W to 2.0W per core; the same 256 cores at 600W target cloud and mainstream data center throughput at 1.7W to 3.5W per core; and the 96-core parts at 500W and 600W serve HPC head nodes and latency-sensitive work at 5W to 10W per core with the headroom to reach 5.3GHz. The 9996 and 9686F we tested sit at the second and third of those points.

Venice also brings three platform-level power controls, starting with Unified Power Provisioning, which sets one budget across the SoC and its DIMMs so a rack can reclaim stranded capacity; AMD says 15% to 25% of rack capacity typically goes unused. AMD’s launch model puts 16 two-socket 9996 servers in a 35kW rack at the default 830W budget for each SoC and its DIMMs, and nearly 19 with that budget set 15% lower at 706W, for a 1% average performance cost.

Utilization-Based Power Scaling lets socket power track the active core count, holding full power in reserve for bursts, and Frequency Adaptive Spectrum Technology sets a floor frequency per core group so one physical part can be sold in several performance tiers. None of the three affected our testing at default power, and we will look at how OEMs expose them as firmware matures.

The Venice lineup is powered by AMD’s Zen 6 and Zen 6c core chiplets, both built on TSMC’s N2 process. Compared with the Zen 5 and Zen 5c designs in Turin, these new core complex dies, or CCDs, offer higher core counts and larger caches.

It helps to know up front that Zen 6 and Zen 6c are not two different designs in the way Intel’s P-cores and E-cores are. AMD builds both on the same microarchitecture, with every feature and every data path shared between the two. Zen 6c is a physically compacted implementation that trades clock speed for area and power, so it can pack far more cores onto a die. AMD lists a maximum frequency of 5.3GHz for Zen 6, up from 5.0GHz on Zen 5, and 4.1GHz for Zen 6c, up from 3.7GHz on Zen 5c.

The standard Zen 6 CCD grows from Turin’s eight Zen 5 cores to twelve. Each core keeps 1MB of private L2, giving the CCD 12MB of aggregate L2, while the shared L3 that all twelve cores draw from rises from 32MB to 48MB. That keeps the ratio at 4MB of L3 per core, the same as Zen 5, so the larger die adds capacity without diluting the cache available to each core.

Zen 6c makes the larger jump, doubling the sixteen cores in Turin’s Zen 5c CCD to 32 and quadrupling shared L3 from 32MB to 128MB, which also doubles the L3 per core from 2MB to 4MB. Each core retains its 1MB L2, bringing the CCD’s aggregate L2 capacity to 32MB. Eight of these CCDs give the 9996 its 256 cores and 512 threads, along with 256MB of total L2 and 1,024MB of L3.

That structure matters for how AMD frames its performance claims. AMD’s headline figure is a geomean IPC uplift of about 27% for Zen 6c over Zen 5 across AI and server workloads. IPC, or instructions per cycle, describes how much work a core completes in each clock tick, independent of frequency. AMD splits that result into two geomeans: about 20% for enterprise and cloud server workloads and about 31% for AI workloads. AMD highlights that these were measured at a fixed frequency, comparing 16 Zen 5 cores spread across two CCDs with 16 Zen 6c cores in a single CCD.

Coming back closer to the execution units, each Zen 6c core has a 32KB, 8-way L1 instruction cache and a 48KB, 12-way L1 data cache. Associativity describes how many locations within the cache a given memory address is allowed to occupy; higher associativity reduces the chance that two frequently used pieces of data keep evicting each other. The only current-generation competitor, NVIDIA’s Vera with its Olympus core, carries 64KB of instruction cache, 96KB of data cache, and 2MB of private L2 per core.

The front end is the part of the core responsible for keeping the execution engine supplied with instructions. It predicts where the program will go next, fetches the instruction bytes from that location, and decodes them into internal operations the core can schedule. Interpreters, database engines, and large server applications make this demanding work, because their short blocks of code frequently end in branches that change the next fetch address. A taken branch sends execution to its target, while a not-taken branch continues through the sequential instructions that follow it. Every time the front end guesses wrong, the work fetched down the wrong path has to be thrown away.

To guess well, Zen 6c uses a TAGE predictor, and AMD says its prediction tables have been tuned for Zen 6 and the branch prediction queues enlarged. The predictor can produce two taken predictions per cycle and up to three prediction windows per cycle. A 64-entry return-address stack, up from 52 on Zen 5c, tracks where function calls should return.

The core follows the predicted route and recovers when a prediction proves wrong, and AMD says Zen 6 shortens that recovery by reducing branch misprediction latency. Vera matches the two-taken-branches-per-cycle ceiling with a neural predictor and specialized prediction mechanisms. Both designs can therefore look ahead through more than one predicted redirect per cycle, which helps instruction delivery keep pace with code that frequently changes direction.

Once the path is predicted, the instruction bytes have to arrive. Zen 6c feeds two 32-byte fetch streams, 64 bytes per cycle in total, from its 32KB L1 instruction cache into paired four-wide decoders. Olympus fetches 128 bytes per cycle and uses a ten-wide decoder, giving Vera the wider fetch and decode path. The two instruction sets encode work differently: x86 instructions vary in length and can carry more work per instruction, while Arm instructions are fixed-length. Those widths therefore describe instruction supply and do not fix a relationship between application throughput on the two cores.

AMD also gives Zen 6c a 6.75K-operation cache, up from 6K on Zen 5c, that holds previously decoded work. Decoding x86 is one of the more power-hungry jobs in the core, so skipping it is valuable. An op cache hit supplies the operation queue directly, taking repeated decoding out of the path.

The cache can deliver up to 18 operations per cycle to that queue, up from 12, comfortably ahead of the eight-wide dispatch stage. Hot loops can keep reusing those operations, which frees the decoders from rebuilding the same work on every pass. AMD also increased op fusion in Zen 6, combining certain pairs of operations into one so they consume less space in the queues downstream.

After the front end, the core has a stream of operations in program order, but there is no rule that they must execute in that order. Out-of-order execution lets the core run any operation whose inputs are ready, even if older instructions are still waiting. To make that safe, the core first performs register renaming. Programs reuse a small set of architectural register names over and over; renaming maps each new value onto one of a much larger pool of physical registers, so independent instructions that happen to reuse the same name do not have to wait on each other.

Zen 6c’s eight-wide rename and dispatch stage feeds 352 integer physical registers, up from 240 on Zen 5c. A 640-entry reorder buffer, up from 448, tracks every operation in flight. The reorder buffer is the bookkeeping structure that lets operations finish out of order while the core still commits results in the original program order. Its size sets how far ahead of a stalled instruction the core can search for independent work.

Between dispatch and the execution units sit the schedulers, which hold operations until their inputs are ready. Here AMD made a structural change: Zen 5 used a unified integer scheduler, and Zen 6 splits it, with 96 entries shared between arithmetic (ALU) and address-generation (AGU) work plus 48 entries dedicated to ALU operations. Zen 5c had 88 ALU entries and 56 AGU entries. AMD also enlarged the floating-point schedulers, and the result is more total scheduling capacity, so more operations can wait for their inputs without stalling dispatch.

That scheduling window lets a database worker overlap independent lookups, for example, or continue arithmetic while an earlier load waits for data. Olympus uses ten-wide allocation to supply its execution machinery and adds value prediction and memory renaming to help advance through dependencies.

Zen 6c’s integer engine includes six ALUs, two integer multipliers, and three branch execution units. Those branch units resolve the actual outcome of each branch after the front end has already predicted the path. Olympus has four branch execution units alongside its wider allocation and commit machinery. The resources address different parts of instruction processing, because predicting a branch early and resolving it during execution are separate jobs.

Vector, or SIMD, instructions apply one operation to many data elements at once, which makes them central to numerical work, compression, media, and increasingly AI inference. AMD’s native 512-bit vector engine returns in both Zen 6 and Zen 6c, meaning a single AVX-512 instruction operates on the full 512-bit register in one pass, with no split into two halves. The execution hardware includes two multiply/FMA pipelines, two add pipelines, and four VNNI INT8 pipelines, double the two on Zen 5.

The biggest change is full AVX-512 FP16 arithmetic: Zen 5 could only convert half-precision values, and Zen 6 computes on them directly. For software that can use half-precision arithmetic, a 512-bit vector holds 32 FP16 values against sixteen FP32 values.

Zen 6 adds several other instruction-set extensions aimed at the same workloads: AVX-512 BMM, a new set of bit matrix multiply instructions; AVX-VNNI-INT8, more INT8 dot-product instructions in the VEX encoding; AVX-NE-CONVERT, for converting BF16 and FP16 values to FP32; and AVX-IFMA, integer fused multiply-add promoted to the VEX encoding. Existing AVX-512 support, including BF16 and VNNI-INT16, carries over from Zen 5. Software needs compiler and library support to use these extensions.

Vera takes a different approach, with six 128-bit SVE2 execution units and FP8 support. Venice has the wider native vectors, while Vera has six narrower units available to process SIMD instructions. The useful comparison depends on the arithmetic a workload needs: FP16 calculations, INT8 dot products, and FP8 operations use different instructions and place different demands on the execution hardware.

Both designs specify a two-cycle latency for floating-point addition. That matters when each addition needs the result of the one before it, since a wide vector engine still has to wait for those dependencies. Vector search and numerical workloads can benefit from Venice’s width when their code exposes enough parallel work and uses data types that fit the available pipelines, and our GROMACS results below show what that looks like in practice.

A 512-bit vector engine is only as fast as the data feeding it, and that job falls to the load/store unit. Zen 6c has four load/store pipelines that can handle a mix of up to four loads and two stores per cycle. For vector code, that works out to two 512-bit or four 256-bit loads per cycle, where Zen 5 managed two loads of any size, along with one 512-bit or two 256-bit stores, subject to the instruction mix.

An 80-entry load queue and a 128-entry store queue, up from 64 and 96 on Zen 5c, keep requests in flight, alongside a scalable load-ordering queue. A load that hits in the L1 data cache has a specified four-cycle latency, and the L1 exchanges data with the L2 over a 64-byte-per-cycle fill and victim path.

Every load also needs its virtual address translated to a physical one, and the translation lookaside buffers, or TLBs, cache those translations so the core does not have to walk the page tables on every access. Zen 6 has a 96-entry L1 data TLB backed by a 4K-entry L2 data TLB that covers every page size except 1GB pages. Large in-memory databases and analytics engines with scattered access patterns lean heavily on TLB reach.

Those queues give the core room to overlap independent memory accesses. Following a chain of pointers is more difficult, because one load has to return before the next address is known. Vera’s Olympus core tackles some of that work with a graph prefetcher that recognizes patterns such as A[B[i]], where an index fetched from one array identifies the element needed from another, giving the hardware a chance to fetch that second value ahead of demand.

A miss in L1 sends the request further through the cache hierarchy. The core’s 16-way private L2 and its CCD’s shared L3 provide the next opportunities to find the data, with requests traveling through the I/O die when they need to reach memory. This is where Venice’s chiplet layout starts to affect how long a core waits for its operands. Meanwhile, the core keeps executing independent operations out of order to keep its units busy. Completed instructions then retire in program order so the software sees the expected sequence of results; Zen 6c has eight-wide retirement against Olympus’s ten-wide commit stage.

Moving beyond the CCDs, the cores need a way to reach memory, devices, and each other. In every EPYC since Rome, that job has belonged to a separate I/O die, or IOD, and Venice splits it across two. Each IOD carries eight DDR5 memory channels, 48 lanes of 64Gb/s SerDes, and eight lanes of slower 16Gb/s SerDes for auxiliary I/O. A SerDes, short for serializer/deserializer, is the high-speed transceiver that carries PCIe, CXL, and socket-to-socket traffic.

In the full eight-CCD package, four CCDs attach to each IOD, and the two IODs are identical dies rotated 180 degrees relative to each other. They sit on a 6nm-class process, while the CCDs moved to 2nm, because analog I/O circuitry gains little from the newest nodes.

How the chiplets talk to each other has also changed. AMD uses Elevated Fanout Bridges, or EFB, for communication between dies, aiming to lower the energy and latency of those transfers. Previous EPYC generations ran die-to-die links through serial connections across the organic package substrate. EFB places a small, dense bridge under the die edges, allowing many more short, wide connections. AMD says this cuts the energy per bit and frees power for the cores. The links run AMD’s fifth-generation Infinity Fabric, which also adds faster fabric power-state changes so the interconnect can drop to lower power when traffic is light.

That gives each half of the processor dedicated memory controllers, I/O, security, and fabric resources. A CCD reaches its local memory controllers through the IOD it connects to, and accessing controllers on the other IOD adds another hop over Infinity Fabric and the latency that comes with it. The NPS settings let software use this division when placing threads and their memory.

Together, the two IODs give SP7 sixteen memory channels at one DIMM per channel. DDR5 RDIMMs run at up to 8,000MT/s, producing a theoretical 1.024TB/s of bandwidth. MRDIMMs take the interface to 12,800MT/s and lift that ceiling to 1.6384TB/s, the basis for AMD’s headline 1.6TB/s figure.

An MRDIMM, or multiplexed-rank DIMM, gets its speed from buffers on the module that combine traffic from multiple ranks onto the faster host interface, increasing the amount of data the channels can carry. Random-access latency still depends on the memory timings and the route taken to reach it. SP7 also has room for up to 8TB of memory using sixteen 512GB 3DS RDIMMs.

Against the competition, Vera’s replaceable LPDDR5X SOCAMM2 modules support up to 1.5TB of memory and up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth, placing it between Venice’s RDIMM and MRDIMM bandwidth ceilings. How far that bandwidth goes also depends on the core count. Dividing the headline figures gives about 6.4GB/s per core for a 256-core Venice with MRDIMMs, 17.1GB/s for a 96-core Venice at the same memory rate, and 13.6GB/s for 88-core Vera. The memory channels are shared, so individual cores do not receive a fixed allocation, but the calculation does help explain why the 9996 and 9686F can have very different demands on the same SP7 memory subsystem.

When sixteen channels of DRAM are not enough, capacity can grow over CXL. SP7 also carries CXL 3.1 on up to 96 of its PCIe Gen6 lanes per socket, and AMD rates each x16 link at about 128GB/s of raw bandwidth at one NUMA hop of latency, which is the path to memory beyond the sixteen channels when capacity matters more than speed.

The same 64Gb/s lanes serve PCIe Gen6: a single-socket SP7 system gets 96 Gen6 lanes plus eight bonus PCIe Gen4 lanes, and a two-socket system gets up to 128 Gen6 lanes plus 16 Gen4 lanes. Links can bifurcate down to x16, x8, x4, or x2. The IODs also support Smart Data Cache Injection, which can steer incoming device data directly into cache, and the Smart Data Accelerator Interface for offloading memory copies.

articles.title: Dell PowerEdge R9825 Review: 512 Venice Cores in an Air-Cooled 3U Server
articles.summary: The most visible of those choices is the height. Dell’s dual-socket mainstream platforms have been 2U for a decade, and the R7725 that this server replaces at the top of the AMD line is a 2U box. The R9825 is 3U, and the extra rack unit buys the airflow room needed to cool two 600W processors with fans alone, so that a customer with a conventional data center can deploy 512-core nodes without a liquid loop.
bodyEvidence: The Dell PowerEdge R9825 is the first server built on AMD’s 6th Gen EPYC to reach our lab, and it is the dual-socket flagship of Dell’s 18th generation PowerEdge line. Two EPYC 9996 processors give it 512 Zen 6c cores and 1,024 threads, 32 DDR5 slots take it to 8TB of memory, and the front panel holds up to 32 E3.S Gen6 x4 NVMe drives. Dell describes it as a high-density dual-socket server engineered for existing air-cooled data center environments, and the design choices that follow from that one sentence are what make the R9825 interesting beyond its core count.

The most visible of those choices is the height. Dell’s dual-socket mainstream platforms have been 2U for a decade, and the R7725 that this server replaces at the top of the AMD line is a 2U box. The R9825 is 3U, and the extra rack unit buys the airflow room needed to cool two 600W processors with fans alone, so that a customer with a conventional data center can deploy 512-core nodes without a liquid loop.

Our review unit shipped with two EPYC 9996 and 2TB of DDR5 running at 8,000MT/s, which we paired with Solidigm Gen5 E3.S drives, and its processor results are in our AMD EPYC Venice SP7 review ; this review is about the server around them.

Dell lists the R9825 at 5.17 inches tall, 17.09 inches wide, and 34.44 inches deep with the bezel, at 94 pounds configured. The depth and weight are in line with a loaded 2U two-socket server; the height is the departure. Inside, Dell has stacked the two processor boards one above the other, where a 2U design lays both sockets side by side across a single board, and that is how the 3U volume turns into cooling headroom.

The height follows from AMD’s socket as much as from Dell’s design. Venice ships on two platforms, and the R9825 uses SP7, the larger one: a 76mm by 80mm socket rated to 600W with sixteen memory channels at one DIMM per channel, which is where the 256-core parts and the 1.6TB/s MRDIMM ceiling live. SP8, due in the first half of 2027, is the smaller enterprise socket, capped at 400W, 128 cores, and eight channels, with more PCIe lanes per socket. That makes the R9825 the top of Dell’s Venice line, and it leaves the volume 2U two-socket role to the PowerEdge R7825, a two-socket EPYC 9006 server Dell lists as coming soon.
Each processor gets a dedicated path for intake air and a full-height heatsink on its tier, and the fan wall behind the drive bays pushes through both tiers.

The front of the chassis is where the airflow design shows. The perforations across the front panel look irregular at first glance, as if Dell had cut a pattern for appearance. They’re actually a purpose-built intake map: the openings line up with the two processor boards, and the density of the pattern is tuned to equalize pressure between the upper and lower tiers so each board receives the same volume of air. Dell’s engineers walked us through the pattern on a site visit, and every part of it is there for thermal reasons.

The lower motherboard follows much of the same layout, with the power supplies and distribution boards flanking it on each side. Those additional components raised the measured temperature of the lower CPU by more than 10C over the upper CPU under our heaviest sustained workloads. The gap narrowed under moderate loads, but it is a wider spread than we have seen on conventional server designs with the two CPUs side by side.

Storage occupies the rest of the front panel. Dell offers the R9825 with 8 or 16 E3.S Gen6 NVMe bays at launch, for a maximum of 983TB, and lists a 32-bay configuration for 1.96PB that is not available at product launch. Every configuration is PCIe Gen6 end to end from the drive to the processor.

Boot comes from a BOSS-N1 or N2 module with two M.2 NVMe SSDs in hardware RAID 1, and PERC H975i and H965i controllers are available for customers who want hardware RAID over the front bays. Our unit used Solidigm 12.8TB Gen5 E3.S drives, which link at Gen5 x4 in Gen6 slots. An upcoming review will look at Gen6 storage performance via Micron SSDs.

Around back, the R9825 offers up to eight PCIe Gen6 x16 slots alongside a Gen4 x4 OCP 3.0 slot, with an option for two Gen6 x8 OCP slots in its place. Accelerator support is modest by design: up to six 75W single-wide, half-length cards, or up to two 675W double-wide full-length cards, which Dell supports only when the server is configured with a single CPU. That positions the R9825 as a CPU-first platform with room for NICs, DPUs, and inference cards, and leaves the heavy GPU work to Dell’s XE line.
Rear ports are a dedicated 1GbE BMC port, two USB 3.1 Type A, and VGA, with a USB Type C, optional USB 2.0 Type A, and mini DisplayPort on the front.

Power supplies run from 1,500W to 3,200W in hot-swap redundant pairs, all Titanium rated, in 100 to 240VAC, 200 to 240VAC, and 277VAC / 336V HVDC variants, plus a 1,400W negative 48V DC option. Two 600W processors, 32 DIMMs, and 32 NVMe drives make the 3,200W units the realistic choice for a full build. Cooling is up to five hot-swappable fans, with direct liquid cooling available as an option.

Dell’s published thermal limits back the air-cooling claim: every processor Dell lists for the chassis, from the 300W, 64-core EPYC 9556 to the 600W EPYC 9996 and 9686F, is supported on air at inlet temperatures up to 35°C with the high-performance fans, across every riser layout and the 8- and 16-bay drive configurations. At 40°C, Dell lists no processor restriction, but MRDIMMs, RDIMMs of 96GB or larger, and GPUs are no longer supported.

At 45°C, processors of 300W or more are not supported on air, which rules out every part on Dell’s list, and that is where the direct liquid cooling option comes in, since it carries no processor restriction at that temperature. The same list confirms the alternatives to the 256-core flagship in this chassis: 192-core, 168-core, and 128-core parts, plus 96-core and 64-core parts in both standard and 5GHz F-series form.

Venice also brings three platform power controls, which we describe in the processor review: a unified SoC and DIMM power budget that AMD models at 16 two-socket 9996 servers per 35kW rack at the default 830W per socket and nearly 19 with the limit set 15% lower, utilization-based power scaling that lets socket power follow the active core count, and a per-core-group frequency floor that turns one physical part into several performance tiers.

Management is iDRAC10 with iDRAC Direct on the front USB port, the Redfish-based RESTful API, RACADM, the iDRAC Service Module, and Dell’s update tooling from Repository Manager through the Server Update Utility. The security list carries signed firmware, self-encrypting drive support, Secure Boot, Secured Component Verification for supply-chain attestation, and Secure Enterprise Key Manager, and Dell describes the platform as post-quantum cryptography ready.

Our unit shipped with iDRAC10 Enterprise at firmware 2.00.05.10, and the feature set matches the PowerEdge R7725 that precedes it. Pages load faster than they did on iDRAC9, but some of the character of earlier versions is gone: server visualizations such as the storage backplane view have become generic dropdown lists, and we hope they return, because those touches set PowerEdge apart from white-box servers.

The component views line up with what the suite recorded: both EPYC 9996 report as Model 81, Stepping 0, with 256 cores each, every DIMM shows as 64GB dual-rank DDR5 at 8,000MT/s and the Micron 9650 E3.S drive in bay 1 reports a negotiated PCIe link of 64GT/s at x4 with NVMe 2.1 and NVMe-MI 2.0 sideband management, confirming Gen6 capabilities.

The full processor evaluation is in the AMD EPYC Venice SP7 review . Here we pull the results that speak to the R9825 as a server, against three systems from our lab. The 2U PowerEdge R7725 is the server it succeeds, with two 192-core EPYC 9965 and 3TB of DDR5-6400 on twelve memory channels per socket to the R9825’s sixteen. The two-socket NVIDIA Vera reference system, with 176 cores and 1.5TB of LPDDR5X-9600, is its direct competitor in the air-cooled two-socket class, and the PowerEdge R770AP with two 120-core Xeon 6978P is Intel’s current top part in our lab.

The other two configurations in the charts ran remotely. AMD gave us SSH access to Nigeria, an AMD-built two-socket SP7 reference server in AMD’s lab, which we ran once with the same pair of EPYC 9996 on MRDIMM-12800 and once with two 96-core, 5.0GHz EPYC 9686F on the same memory. The 9996 run is the closest look available at the R9825’s MRDIMM option, because the processors match and the memory moves from 8,000MT/s to 12,800MT/s. Those runs are the only data here not collected in our lab, and the platform differs from the Dell in chassis, firmware, and data drive, so we present them as a guide to the memory option.

Results come from our sr-suite and sr-harness methodology. The R9825, the AMD reference platform, and Vera ran Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15.2, with the Venice systems in NPS2 and SMT on and off; the R7725 and R770AP were tested earlier on Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 13.3, which leaves them a small compiler handicap against the newer systems.

Memory bandwidth is the figure that defines what the R9825 can and can’t do at 512 cores. With its 32 DDR5 modules running at 8,000MT/s, the system sustained 1,201GB/s on STREAM Triad with SMT off, 1.9x the R7725’s 634GB/s on 24 channels of DDR5-6400, with one socket reading its local memory at 602GB/s and the remote socket at 148GB/s over xGMI. That generational multiple leans on a low R7725 result, because the suite’s STREAM build doesn’t count the extra read AMD’s Zen cores make on every store; the harness STREAM Copy test, which avoids it, puts the gap at 1,158GB/s against 832GB/s.

Vera’s LPDDR5X system reached 2,073GB/s, and the same two EPYC 9996 on MRDIMM-12800 in AMD’s reference platform reached 1,901GB/s, which is the configuration a bandwidth-bound buyer should spec from Dell. Local latency of 87.6ns at 2MB pages is the best in the group.

HPC is where 512 cores and sixteen channels per socket show up together. GROMACS benchPEP, the 12-million-atom molecular dynamics case run across every physical core, finished at 9.72 ns/day on the R9825 against 5.36 for the R7725 and 2.07 for Vera with SMT on, a 1.8x generational gain for Dell’s AMD flagship and 4.7x the Arm system. The large OpenFOAM mesh, a 22.6-million-cell CFD solve that outruns every cache, took 1,036 seconds on the R9825 against 2,678 on the R7725 and 1,854 on Vera; on MRDIMMs the same processors finished in 815 seconds, a 21% cut that is the clearest argument for the faster memory option.

Scale-out data work follows the core count, and one 256-core socket moved 76.5M Valkey GET and 74.2M SET requests per second at a pipeline depth of 16, 27% and 65% more than one 192-core EPYC 9965 socket and 3.4x Vera’s 88-core socket. ClickBench’s hot sum on ClickHouse, which does not scale past 192 cores, was a tie at 2.69 seconds against 2.70 for the R7725, with Vera at 2.09; the cold sum of 5.75 seconds matched Vera’s 5.70 and beat the R7725’s 9.61, where the older system’s drive sits on a Gen5 x2 link.

The harness throughput tests with SMT on put a number on 1,024 threads. The R9825 compressed at 2,034 GIPS and decompressed at 3,400 GIPS in 7-Zip, 33% and 63% ahead of the R7725 and 2.1x and 2.3x Vera, and OpenSSL AES-256-GCM across all threads reached 6.8TB/s against 3.96TB/s on the R7725 and 1.26TB/s on Vera. On a single pinned thread, a Zen 6c core at 4.1GHz compressed at 11,068 MIPS against 7,077 for Zen 5c and 9,537 for Olympus, and the Linux kernel allmodconfig build finished in 99.4 seconds with SMT off against 146.2 on the R7725.

Two results go the other way, and both are thread-count effects. The Renaissance JVM suite and schbench penalize a 1,024-thread system because the JVM and the scheduler benchmark spread work across every logical CPU they see, so the R9825 trails smaller systems there, and Vera’s remote-socket bandwidth of 677GB/s over NVLink-C2C is 4.6x the 148GB/s the R9825’s xGMI links deliver, which makes NPS2 placement and NUMA-aware software more important on this server than on the Arm one. Full tables for both are in the processor review.

For databases, Steve Shaw of HammerDB ran TPROC-C on HammerDB 6.1.1 against a single EPYC 9996 socket in the R9825, 256 cores with SMT off, at 2,048 warehouses, alongside Vera’s 88-core socket at 1,408, a two-socket EPYC 9175F system at 512, and one 96-core EPYC 9686F socket on AMD’s reference platform at 768.

The R9825 socket peaked at 2.39M new orders per minute on MySQL 26.10, 2.60M on VillageSQL, 2.26M on MariaDB 13.0.2, and 2.61M on PostgreSQL 18.6, winning MySQL by 14% over Vera, tying VillageSQL, and trailing by 11% to 12% on the other two. The PostgreSQL peak arrived with the socket 18% busy, so the database set the ceiling and the server had headroom to spare; the full analysis is in the Venice review.

The 96-core EPYC 9686F, the fourth system in the chart, posted the round’s highest PostgreSQL result at 3.03M NOPM, ahead of Vera’s 2.90M, and reached 2.28M on MariaDB, 2.10M on VillageSQL, and 1.84M on MySQL.

Tail latency at a matched load of 144 virtual users went to the R9825 on every engine. PAYMENT p99 ran 2.87ms on MariaDB, 1.91ms on MySQL, 1.37ms on VillageSQL, and 1.48ms on PostgreSQL, against 4.11ms, 3.16ms, 2.82ms, and 2.34ms on Vera, which puts the R9825’s tails 30% to 51% lower. The chart shows only these two systems because they are the only ones Shaw ran to 144 users; the 96-core EPYC 9686F profile topped out at 104 users and the two-socket EPYC 9175F system at 68, loads sized to their core counts.

The PowerEdge R9825 is the server AMD’s 256-core Venice needed: a mainstream, air-cooled two-socket box that an enterprise can rack next to the R7725 and R770 without changing to a liquid loop. Dell took the dual-socket flagship to 3U, stacked the processor boards, and shaped the intake around them so two 600W processors run on five fans, and the payoff is 512 cores in a chassis that doubles the R7725’s HPC throughput, beats it by 27% to 65% on compression and key-value work, and ships with PCIe Gen6 from the slots to the drive bays.

The configuration decision that matters most is memory. Our review unit ran its memory at 8,000MT/s and sustained 1,201GB/s on STREAM Triad; RDIMMs at that speed are the capacity choice at up to 8TB, while the MRDIMM-12800 option halves the capacity ceiling and lifts bandwidth toward 1.9TB/s, and for CFD and other memory-bound HPC it matters about as much as the core count, cutting the large OpenFOAM solve by 21% on the same processors. Buyers whose workloads synchronize across every thread, as JVM services and some scheduler-bound code do, should look at the 96-core and 128-core Venice parts in the same chassis.

The third rack unit has a cost in density on core-bound work. At 512 cores in 3U, the R9825 holds 171 cores per rack unit against 192 for an R7725 with two EPYC 9965, and it delivers about 11% less 7-Zip compression throughput per rack unit even as it wins by 33% per server. On memory-bound and vector work, the extra height pays off, with GROMACS 21% higher and the large OpenFOAM mesh about 1.7x per rack unit, so the case for the R9825 is strongest where memory bandwidth and air cooling set the limit.

Against NVIDIA’s Vera, the first serious Arm competitor in this class, the R9825 wins most of the board on raw performance and loses on memory bandwidth, ClickBench’s hot sum, PostgreSQL and MariaDB throughput, and a few latency-bound single-thread tests, which is the processor story told in full in the Venice review. On HammerDB, a single EPYC 9996 socket kept pace with a full Vera socket on OLTP throughput and beat it on tail latency by 30% to 51%, with the database engines setting the ceiling.

For delivering 512 Zen 6c cores, up to 8TB of memory, and PCIe Gen6 from the slots to the drive bays in an air-cooled 3U chassis that any existing data center can deploy, the Dell PowerEdge R9825 earns our Best Overall Server award.

bodyEvidence: DapuStor announced the J5101, an enterprise NVMe M.2 boot SSD for AI, HPC, virtualization, and cloud servers. The drive uses a PCIe Gen4 interface in the M.2 2280 form factor, comes in 480GB, 960GB, and 1.92TB capacities, and carries power loss protection and a 1 DWPD endurance rating. DapuStor rates it at 2W idle and as little as 4.5W active, and says it is in volume production and running in customer environments.

DapuStor positions the J5101 as a replacement for PXE network boot and SATA boot drives. A local NVMe boot device gives each node dedicated storage for the operating system, which the company says makes startup and recovery more dependable as the software stack on AI nodes grows. Because an M.2 2280 drive does not occupy a front-accessible bay, those bays stay available for primary data storage in dense AI servers where internal space is tight.

DapuStor lists sequential reads of up to 3,800MB/s and 4KB random reads of up to 650,000 IOPS, with endurance rated at 1 drive write per day (DWPD). The company has not published write performance or the NAND type. It says the three capacities let customers match the drive to each system’s boot requirements without paying for capacity they will not use.

DapuStor leads with power draw: the drive idles at 2W, and its active power starts at 4.5W. In the company’s comparison of 960GB enterprise M.2 boot drives, the J5101 draws 5.5W active and 2W idle, against 8.9W and 3.5W for one unnamed competitor and 8W and 3W for another. That works out to 31% to 38% less active power and 33% to 43% less at idle. These are vendor figures, and we did not run or audit them.

DapuStor’s pitch is that small per-drive savings add up across thousands of servers. Boot drives typically spend most of their life near idle, so the idle gap is the one that counts: 1W to 1.5W per drive in DapuStor’s comparison, which comes to 1kW to 1.5kW across 1,000 servers with one boot drive each, and twice that where boot drives are mirrored.

The J5101 includes power loss protection (PLP) and end-to-end data protection to guard the boot volume against unexpected power interruptions, and Secure Boot support and firmware integrity checks protect the boot process and the drive firmware. DapuStor also cites 4K error correction and ASIC-accelerated machine learning, which it says reduce NAND retries and adapt to varying NAND operating conditions. Keeping the operating system on a dedicated boot device separates it from the application data drives, which the company counts as part of the reliability case.

The J5101 is in volume production, and DapuStor says customers are running it in production environments. It brings the J5 family, which DapuStor otherwise lists as U.2 and add-in card drives such as the J5060 QLC SSD we reviewed , to the M.2 boot slot. DapuStor’s SC26 lineup at booth 1702 in Chicago includes the J5 M.2 boot SSD alongside the 512TB R6060 QLC SSD it first demonstrated at FMS 2026.

articles.title: NVIDIA Vera CPU Review: 2TB/s of Memory Bandwidth and a Real Challenger to x86
articles.summary: Its successor, Vera, is far more ambitious. It is a clean-sheet design built around Olympus, NVIDIA’s custom Arm core. Olympus implements Armv9.2, and each Vera CPU features 88 cores and 176 threads. Alongside the new cores, the memory subsystem is the other highlight. Each CPU supports up to 1.5TB of LPDDR5X on SOCAMM modules, with an advertised peak bandwidth of 1.2TB/s per socket, which gives Vera the power efficiency of mobile-class DRAM while keeping the memory field-replaceable. Across the two sockets in our test server, that rating comes to 2.4TB/s, and we measured 2,073GB/s on STREAM Triad.
bodyEvidence: For most of its time in the data center, NVIDIA treated the CPU as little more than the chip that fed the GPU. Grace, its first server processor, fit that mold. It used Arm’s off-the-shelf Neoverse V2 cores and shipped mostly as the CPU half of the Grace Hopper and Grace Blackwell superchips. Those superchips did introduce one lasting piece of the platform: NVLink-C2C, a link that gives the CPU and GPU coherent access to each other’s memory at far higher bandwidth than PCIe.

Its successor, Vera, is far more ambitious. It is a clean-sheet design built around Olympus, NVIDIA’s custom Arm core. Olympus implements Armv9.2, and each Vera CPU features 88 cores and 176 threads. Alongside the new cores, the memory subsystem is the other highlight. Each CPU supports up to 1.5TB of LPDDR5X on SOCAMM modules, with an advertised peak bandwidth of 1.2TB/s per socket, which gives Vera the power efficiency of mobile-class DRAM while keeping the memory field-replaceable. Across the two sockets in our test server, that rating comes to 2.4TB/s, and we measured 2,073GB/s on STREAM Triad.

That ambition extends to where Vera is deployed. It still ships as part of the superchip in Vera Rubin systems, but NVIDIA has also expanded it to its BlueField-4 STX storage platform and to standalone CPU servers for agentic sandboxes. Vera is also gaining broad support from OEMs, hyperscalers, and NCPs: Dell, HPE, and Supermicro have added Vera servers to their lineups, and hyperscalers and NCPs are poised to make it a mainstream offering. That broad availability matters because, as our results will show, Vera is a serious contender against its x86 counterparts, and it gives organizations a third CPU vendor to help diversify their supply chains.

To understand why Vera matters to NVIDIA, look at how the company has grown. NVIDIA built its data center position around the GPU, then expanded into the infrastructure needed to keep those GPUs running. On the hardware side, the 2020 Mellanox acquisition brought the networking technology that connects servers and moves data between them. On the software side, CUDA, DOCA, and the wider software stack extended NVIDIA’s reach into how that hardware is programmed and operated. Together, those pieces gave the company control over much of the accelerated computing platform.

But the platform still needed a general-purpose CPU. Something had to run the operating system, prepare data, manage applications, and coordinate the work sent to the accelerators. During much of NVIDIA’s expansion, Intel and AMD filled that role. That left NVIDIA in an awkward position: it could supply the GPUs, the network, and much of the software while still depending on another company’s processor at the center of the server.

Grace was the first major step toward changing that. Built around Arm Neoverse V2 cores, it gave NVIDIA a data center CPU and a way to connect that CPU more closely to its GPUs through NVLink-C2C. Grace nevertheless left a performance gap to close. Its memory bandwidth and efficiency made it competitive as an AI host CPU, but leading x86 processors retained substantial advantages in most other workloads. That uneven performance limited the argument for choosing Grace as a general-purpose replacement for an EPYC or Xeon server.

Vera closes much of that gap by replacing Grace’s Neoverse V2 cores with NVIDIA’s custom Olympus design and substantially increasing memory bandwidth and capacity. By supplying a competitive CPU alongside its GPUs, DPUs, and networking, NVIDIA can capture a larger share of spending on each server. It also gives the company greater control over its ecosystem and how the components work together: the CPU cores, memory subsystem, interconnect, and GPU can be designed around the same requirements. Vera’s coherent CPU-to-GPU link, now rated at up to 1.8TB/s, is a concrete example of that integration.

Capturing more of each system’s spend is only part of the picture. Reinforcement learning (RL) and agentic AI give NVIDIA another reason to offer a standalone CPU system. An agent does more than generate a response. It calls tools, retrieves information, runs code, and checks the results before deciding what to do next. Much of that execution happens on CPUs, and when the next model step depends on a CPU task’s result, slow execution delays the whole sequence. Per-core performance, memory latency, and predictable behavior under load therefore become important to the responsiveness of the agent.

Those requirements align closely with the design of Vera’s 88 Olympus cores, which are built around a clear priority: strong performance from each core, sustained when the entire socket is busy. Olympus is NVIDIA’s implementation of the Armv9.2 instruction set, replacing the Neoverse V2 cores used in Grace. That distinction matters: Arm defines the instructions the processor runs, while NVIDIA designed the machinery that fetches, schedules, and executes them. That control lets NVIDIA tune the core for its goal: finishing individual tasks quickly while running many at once.

The first half of that goal starts with instructions per cycle, or IPC: how many instructions a core completes, on average, in each clock cycle. Clock speed determines how often those cycles occur; the microarchitecture determines how much useful work can fit into them. NVIDIA claims a 1.5x IPC improvement over its previous generation. The highest clock we observed was 3.41GHz, but Vera’s architecture emphasizes extracting more work per cycle and maintaining that progress under load. That emphasis matters because, for a compiler, interpreter, or database operation with a long sequence of dependent steps, additional cores alone cannot make that sequence finish faster.

Achieving that IPC begins with a steady supply of useful instructions. Olympus’s front end, the part of the core that fetches and decodes program instructions, can decode up to ten instructions per cycle. That width matters only if it stays fed, which becomes difficult when software frequently branches between code paths. Olympus therefore combines a neural branch predictor with other specialized predictors and supports up to two taken branches per cycle. Better prediction helps the core fetch the instructions it will need, reducing time spent executing the wrong path and restarting after a mistake.

Once those instructions are fetched and decoded, Olympus uses out-of-order execution to find work that can proceed while earlier instructions wait. For example, if one operation is waiting for memory, an independent calculation can execute ahead of it. A large instruction window gives the processor more opportunities to find that independent work.

Even so, some sequences, like the dependent chains described above, resist this approach because each step needs the previous step’s result. For those, Olympus also uses value prediction to let dependent operations begin with a predicted value, then checks that value when the actual result becomes available. Correct predictions can reduce the effective wait along these dependency chains; incorrect predictions require the speculative work to be corrected and recomputed.

The execution engine then needs enough capacity to turn that instruction supply into completed work. Olympus combines broad integer execution resources with dedicated branch units, four load pipelines, and two store pipelines. These resources meet different demands: integer units handle arithmetic, comparisons, and logic; branch units resolve control flow; and load/store pipelines move data between the core and its caches. The balance matters because a wider decoder would offer little benefit if instructions simply backed up behind an execution or memory bottleneck.

Alongside those scalar resources, Olympus has six 128-bit vector pipelines supporting SVE2, with FP8 support and cryptographic capabilities in two pipelines. Vector instructions apply an operation to multiple data elements, making them useful for numerical work, compression, and data processing.

This is one area where Olympus makes a clear trade-off: its 128-bit vector width is smaller than the 512-bit width available through AVX-512 on competing x86 processors. The difference matters for optimized numerical kernels and even tokenizers, although application performance also depends on the throughput of the particular instructions, the generated code, and the supply of data. Scientific applications such as GROMACS therefore remain a separate test of the design’s strengths.

Each of these execution resources, scalar or vector, depends on data arriving on time, so keeping frequently used data close to the execution engine matters just as much. Each core has a 64KB instruction cache, a 96KB data cache, and a private 2MB L2 cache. The small first-level caches provide quick access to the most immediately useful instructions and data; the larger L2 retains more of the core’s working set before an access has to travel farther through the processor. Giving every core a substantial private L2 supports the same per-core objective: more work can be serviced locally, reducing pressure on shared cache and main memory.

Prefetching complements those caches by bringing data in before an instruction requests it. Alongside prefetchers for regular access patterns, Olympus includes a graph prefetcher for indirect accesses such as A[B[i]], where one lookup supplies the index for another. After learning that relationship, the hardware can start fetching the second piece of data before the program demands it. This helps address a common problem in graph processing and other irregular workloads: the processor has ample execution capacity, but progress depends on finding the next piece of data.

The final piece of Olympus addresses the other half of its goal: running many tasks at once. Each core supports two hardware threads, giving Vera 176 threads per socket. NVIDIA calls its scheme Spatial Multithreading. The core can devote its resources to one active thread or divide resources between two active threads, providing a choice between concentrating execution capacity on one instruction stream and supporting more concurrent work.

NVIDIA’s stated objective is to reduce interference between the two threads, making performance more predictable when both are busy, which is the same predictability agentic workloads depend on under load. The two threads still share a physical core and the wider memory system, so partitioning resources does not guarantee a fixed application latency.

Beyond the individual core, keeping 88 wide cores productive requires more than a fast connection to DRAM. The cores also need to exchange data, access shared cache, and communicate with attached devices. Vera connects these resources through the second generation of NVIDIA’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, an internal mesh that also keeps cached copies of shared data coherent. The cores, fabric, and 164MB system-level cache sit on one compute die, with memory controllers and I/O on adjacent chiplets. NVIDIA rates the fabric at 3.4TB/s of bisection bandwidth, a measure of traffic capacity across the mesh, separate from main memory bandwidth.

That single-die layout avoids transfers between separate compute dies when cores communicate or access shared cache. For software, Vera also presents one NUMA node per socket: the operating system sees each socket as one group of cores and locally attached memory. This simplifies placement within the socket, although it does not mean every path through the mesh has identical latency. A two-socket server still has two NUMA nodes, and accessing the other socket’s memory remains different from accessing local memory.

Within each socket, the shared system-level cache, or L3, sits one level beyond the private L2 caches described earlier. It gives the cores another chance to reuse data without going to DRAM and provides shared capacity accessible across the socket. Its 164MB is substantial, but some competing processors offer considerably more L3. That matters when a repeatedly accessed working set is too large for a core’s L2 but fits in a larger shared cache. High DRAM bandwidth helps when data must come from memory; it does not remove the benefit of avoiding that access in the first place.
Because that capacity is shared, Vera also supports Arm MPAM, allowing system software to partition shared cache capacity and manage memory-bandwidth allocations between workloads.

When accesses do reach main memory, Vera has considerable bandwidth available. Eight 128-bit LPDDR5X controllers provide a 1,024-bit aggregate interface, with memory running at up to 9,600MT/s for a rated 1.2TB/s per socket. The memory sits on eight removable SOCAMM2 modules, combining LPDDR5X with field-replaceable modules. This gives Vera a broad, fast memory interface without requiring soldered-down memory.

Raw bandwidth is only part of the picture, though. The more useful relationship is between that bandwidth and the number of cores sharing it. Dividing the rated 1.2TB/s by 88 cores gives about 13.6GB/s per physical core. This is a way to describe the processor’s balance, not a dedicated allocation or a guarantee of what each thread receives. Increasing core count without a matching increase in memory bandwidth would reduce that ratio.

Dividing our measured STREAM bandwidth by the number of physical cores gives 11.8GB/s per core on Vera, compared with 3.8GB/s on the 240-core Xeon 6978P system. That is a concrete example of Vera supplying substantial memory throughput relative to its compute resources.

Power efficiency is part of the same design choice. NVIDIA estimates roughly 30W to 40W for a fully populated LPDDR5X memory subsystem, depending on capacity. The appeal of LPDDR5X is to supply this bandwidth while keeping memory’s contribution to total server power low, leaving more of the system’s power and cooling budget available for computation.

Bandwidth and efficiency still say nothing about how much data fits, and capacity remains a separate consideration. NVIDIA specifies up to 1.5TB of directly attached LPDDR5X per socket, or 3TB across two sockets. For workloads that need their working set resident in memory, higher transfer rates cannot compensate for insufficient capacity.

Where that directly attached capacity is not enough, Vera’s I/O provides a path to more, along with connections for devices. The standalone CPU platform provides 88 PCIe Gen6 lanes per socket for networking, storage, and accelerators, while the Vera Rubin configuration exposes 96. On the memory side, CXL 3.1 support includes Type 3 memory devices and memory pooling, allowing capacity to extend beyond the SOCAMM2 modules. That expanded memory uses a different access path from the directly attached LPDDR5X, so its performance must be evaluated separately.

Finally, for communication between processors, Vera uses second-generation NVLink-C2C, the successor to the link introduced with Grace’s superchips. It connects two Vera CPUs in a dual-socket server or links Vera to Rubin GPUs in a superchip. The link provides up to 1.8TB/s of aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, or 900GB/s in each direction, and it reflects the same tight CPU-GPU integration that drives NVIDIA’s push into the CPU business in the first place.

Our review unit is NVIDIA’s MGX Vera C2, a dual-socket, air-cooled 2U reference server that NVIDIA’s partners are using as the basis for their first Vera systems. Eight E1.S bays run across the top of the front panel next to four hot-swap Delta power supplies, with honeycomb intake filling the rest of the face. Because the power supplies load from the front, the rear stays clear for I/O cabling in a rack and is given over to the PCIe risers and management I/O.

Inside, the two Vera CPUs sit side by side under passive heatsinks, with SOCAMM2 modules along their flanks. A wall of six fan modules in the center of the chassis, just behind the drive bays, pulls air across both sockets, and foam blocks between each pair of fans direct the airflow. From a cooling standpoint, the layout is well thought out.

Both processors are mounted directly to the PCB with no socket, the same way NVIDIA ships Vera in its superchips. The 16 SOCAMM2 slots surround the two packages, so the memory remains field-replaceable even though the processors are not; replacing a CPU means swapping the board. Over the summer, we also looked at the liquid-cooled version of the same board, which runs quick-disconnect coolant lines across the top of the board to the processor cold plates while leaving the SOCAMM2 modules air-cooled.
The middle riser holds an NVIDIA ConnectX-8 adapter for up to 800G networking, and the rear panel carries USB, DisplayPort, and a dedicated network port for out-of-band management.

The platform is highly modular and supports a range of storage and rear PCIe configurations, but that flexibility comes at the cost of service time. Its three FHFL PCIe risers look easy to service at first glance. In a typical server, swapping a card means releasing the riser, flipping out a support tab or removing a screw, and sliding the card out.

On the Vera server, you first pop off the fan cover, remove one or more of the foam blocks, and disconnect and lift out the riser’s power and PCIe cables. Only then can the entire riser assembly slide out through the rear of the chassis. Once the sled is free, it has to be disassembled to reach the card and then reassembled after the swap. A job that takes a few seconds on a conventional server takes 5 to 10 minutes per sled here.
In practice, in-rack servicing is off the table unless you are prepared to shuffle back and forth, so most component swaps require moving the server to a bench to service.

The benchmarks examine how Vera’s design translates into performance, from individual threads to workloads using the full system. Our tests cover memory bandwidth and latency, scientific computing, general-purpose software, and databases, showing how the processor handles different demands on its cores and memory system.

We compared Vera against five Dell PowerEdge configurations with ideal memory configuration and tested them with the same suite, covering AMD’s highest-core-count and frequency-optimized EPYC parts along with current- and previous-generation Xeons.

Because Olympus support first arrived in GCC 15, Vera ran a newer software stack than the x86 systems, as listed above. Benchmark versions, inputs, and build flags were otherwise identical across all systems.

Memory is where Vera departs most from x86, so we start our testing there. We tested STREAM Triad, run with one OpenMP thread per physical core on 16GiB arrays. The headline run uses every core in the system, with each thread’s data placed on the same socket. We then repeat it with socket 0’s cores reading first their local memory and then the remote socket’s memory, and with every core reading pages interleaved across both sockets. The chart below shows whole-system Triad results for each server with SMT off.

Vera sustained 2,073GB/s, 86% of its 2.4TB/s two-socket rating. The closest x86 system was the Xeon 6978P, whose 24 channels of DDR5-6400 delivered 914GB/s, 74% of its 1,229GB/s theoretical peak, for a 2.3x Vera lead. The two EPYC systems run the same 24 channels of DDR5-6400 yet landed well below that: 651GB/s for the 32-core 9175F and 634GB/s for the 384-core 9965, just 52% of peak and a 3.3x Vera lead. Finally, the Xeon 6787P and 8592+ trail the pack running on slower DDR5-5200 and DDR5-4800, reaching 479GB/s and 482GB/s.

Part of the EPYC shortfall comes from how STREAM counts traffic. The suite builds STREAM with plain GCC, which doesn’t emit streaming stores, so a store that misses cache first reads its destination line from memory. STREAM doesn’t count that read, which means Triad understates the traffic moved by a quarter wherever it happens. AMD’s Zen cores pay it on every store. Arm cores such as NVIDIA’s earlier Grace detect full-line writes and skip the read, and Intel’s recent Xeons can skip most of it when memory is heavily loaded.

The separate Phoronix Test Suite build of STREAM points the same way. With SMT off, its Copy result reached 832GB/s on the 9965 and 873GB/s on the 9175F, about 1.5x the suite build’s 551GB/s and 570GB/s, and in line with the gain Copy should see once the extra read is gone; on the Xeons, the two builds landed within 9% of each other.

articles.title: Supermicro Plans 10,000 SambaNova SN50 RDUs for GPU-Paired Inference Racks, With GPUs on Prefill and RDUs on Decode
articles.summary: The split follows the two phases of LLM inference. Prefill processes the prompt and is compute-bound, which SambaNova assigns to the NVIDIA GPUs; decode generates the response one token at a time and is memory-bound, which it assigns to the SN50. SambaNova’s case for the pairing is that agentic workloads spend most of their time in decode, because an agent makes thousands of model calls and each response gates its next action, so a faster decode stage shortens the whole loop.
bodyEvidence: SambaNova and Supermicro will build and sell disaggregated inference systems that pair NVIDIA GPUs with SambaNova’s SN50 Reconfigurable Dataflow Units (RDUs), with Supermicro initially planning for 10,000 SN50 chips. The racks join Supermicro’s Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) catalog, and Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver, and support them. Both companies describe the 10,000 chips as a planning figure for a phased rollout; neither has disclosed a purchase commitment, pricing, or a ship date.

The split follows the two phases of LLM inference. Prefill processes the prompt and is compute-bound, which SambaNova assigns to the NVIDIA GPUs; decode generates the response one token at a time and is memory-bound, which it assigns to the SN50. SambaNova’s case for the pairing is that agentic workloads spend most of their time in decode, because an agent makes thousands of model calls and each response gates its next action, so a faster decode stage shortens the whole loop.

SN50 is SambaNova’s fifth-generation RDU, and the company says it serves the largest models at high throughput without extreme rack power density, so operators can add inference capacity in existing facilities and keep GPUs they already own on prefill duty. SambaNova claims 5x the compute per accelerator and 4x the network bandwidth of its previous generation for the SambaRack SN50, which is air-cooled and scales to 256 accelerators.

SambaRack SN50 carries 16 RDUs per rack, so the initial 10,000-chip plan works out to about 625 racks if Supermicro keeps that density. SambaNova has not published throughput, latency, or power figures for the combined GPU and RDU systems, and Supermicro has not specified the server configurations, GPU models, or interconnects, or how many GPUs and RDUs each system holds. Supermicro’s DCBBS catalog already includes the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks and the Vera CPU rack it positions for agent sandboxes.

Supermicro takes system integration, testing, delivery, and customer support, including on-site service, while SambaNova engineers bring models onto SN50, tune them for the hardware, and assist Supermicro with deployments. For buyers, the change is in the channel: SN50 RDUs can be ordered alongside GPUs from Supermicro in the same way as the rest of a rack, with one vendor responsible for the system.

“Agentic AI is the next wave of inference, and it has to run everywhere,” said Rodrigo Liang, co-founder and CEO of SambaNova. “Supermicro builds AI infrastructure for data centers globally. Now customers can order SN50 RDUs alongside GPUs, from a world-leading partner they trust. That’s how fast, efficient inference gets to scale.”

“Our collaboration with SambaNova expands our broad DCBBS portfolio by enabling heterogeneous architectures that integrate GPU computing with specialized inference acceleration, helping customers deploy efficient, scalable AI solutions,” said Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro.

The companies will start with NeoClouds and sovereign clouds, then expand to enterprises running AI on premises. SambaNova expects the partnership to put substantially more high-performance inference capacity into service in 2027 than it could alone, and it has not named customers or given a schedule for the 10,000 chips. The deal follows SambaNova’s July first close of a $1 billion financing at an $11 billion valuation, which came with JPMorganChase deploying SN40 and SN50 systems for on-prem inference, and its heterogeneous inference collaboration with Intel.
