articles.title: Simplyblock Earns Red Hat Certification for OpenShift Virtualization Storage, With Zero-RPO DR Built In
articles.summary: Simplyblock runs as a distributed storage engine inside Kubernetes, pooling NVMe devices across nodes into one block storage pool that serves both containerized services and KubeVirt VMs. Hosts reach volumes over NVMe/TCP or NVMe over RDMA (RoCEv2), and the I/O path is built on the Storage Performance Development Kit (SPDK), which runs in user space to avoid the Linux kernel’s storage overhead. Simplyblock targets sub-millisecond latency and grows capacity by adding nodes to the cluster.
bodyEvidence: Simplyblock’s Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver and Kubernetes operator now carry Red Hat certification and are listed in the Red Hat Ecosystem Catalog, which gives OpenShift Virtualization customers a validated storage layer for VMs moved off VMware vSphere. The software-defined platform runs on servers customers already own, provisions NVMe block volumes for containers and KubeVirt VMs, and includes the replication and disaster recovery features simplyblock added to the platform in September.

Simplyblock runs as a distributed storage engine inside Kubernetes, pooling NVMe devices across nodes into one block storage pool that serves both containerized services and KubeVirt VMs. Hosts reach volumes over NVMe/TCP or NVMe over RDMA (RoCEv2), and the I/O path is built on the Storage Performance Development Kit (SPDK), which runs in user space to avoid the Linux kernel’s storage overhead. Simplyblock targets sub-millisecond latency and grows capacity by adding nodes to the cluster.

Data is protected with distributed erasure coding, which simplyblock says provides the fault tolerance of three-way mirroring at lower raw cost: a 4+2 scheme stores usable capacity at 1.5x raw against 3x for triple replication. The platform also handles thin provisioning, copy-on-write snapshots, writable clones, per-tenant quality of service limits, and volume-level encryption. The Red Hat Ecosystem Catalog lists five certified simplyblock container images, with the operator bundle at version 26.3.0 supporting OpenShift 4.19 through 4.22 and the CSI driver at 26.2.4.

The replication and recovery features simplyblock added in September are part of the certified stack. Synchronous replication across a metro-distance stretch cluster delivers a zero recovery point objective (RPO), and asynchronous replication between clusters reaches RPOs as low as one minute, with delta-based transfers and automated failback. Live forward replication moves running volumes, including VM disks, between clusters without disruption, and point-in-time backups go to any S3-compatible object store for off-site protection.

Simplyblock CEO Rob Pankow says organizations leaving VMware need an OpenShift storage design that covers what vSAN, vMotion, and Site Recovery Manager did for them, and that certified storage with integrated disaster recovery provides it without a separately licensed DR product.

articles.title: AMD Instinct MI350P First Look: 144GB of HBM3E in a 600W PCIe Card
articles.summary: AMD also showcased the MI350P at IFA 2026 in its Threadripper Halo Station prototype, where the same accelerators were liquid-cooled. The workstation concept supports up to four MI350Ps alongside a 96-core Threadripper PRO processor, providing 576GB of aggregate HBM3E capacity in a single machine; AMD’s product page, updated in October, now lists the system as coming in 2027. That gives us two ways to look at the MI350P: as a PCIe accelerator for servers, and as the building block for a larger deskside AI system competing with machines like the GB300 DGX Station.
bodyEvidence: The AMD Instinct MI350P is AMD’s first new PCIe Instinct GPU in four years, following the MI210 in 2022. It brings the company’s CDNA 4 architecture to a conventional add-in card, with up to 4.6 PFLOPS of MXFP4 performance, 144GB of HBM3E, and 4TB/s of memory bandwidth. All of that fits into a dual-slot, 600W air-cooled card, giving customers another way to deploy Instinct GPUs without moving to the larger 8 GPU OAM MI350/5X platform.

AMD also showcased the MI350P at IFA 2026 in its Threadripper Halo Station prototype, where the same accelerators were liquid-cooled. The workstation concept supports up to four MI350Ps alongside a 96-core Threadripper PRO processor, providing 576GB of aggregate HBM3E capacity in a single machine; AMD’s product page, updated in October, now lists the system as coming in 2027. That gives us two ways to look at the MI350P: as a PCIe accelerator for servers, and as the building block for a larger deskside AI system competing with machines like the GB300 DGX Station.

This first look takes the server view, so the comparison that matters for a buyer specifying a PCIe accelerator is the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, the card that sits in the same power class and the same slots, and the H200 NVL is in the charts as the most capable NVIDIA add-in card for the workloads where memory bandwidth decides the result. A single GB300 DGX Station stands in for the deskside view; it is a different class of machine at a different price, and it is there to show how far a full Blackwell Ultra GPU sits above any of the PCIe cards.

AMD’s published numbers put the MI350P’s weight on low precision: 4.6 PFLOPS at MXFP4 and MXFP6, 2.3 PFLOPS at FP8, and 1.15 PFLOPS at FP16 or BF16, all dense figures. The memory system is the other half of the card: 144GB of HBM3E on a 4,096-bit interface at 4TB/s, behind a 128MB Infinity Cache, which is what the single-stream results below lean on. Board power is 600W with a 450W configurable mode; our review unit ran at 450W.

The MI350P uses the same CDNA 4 architecture as the larger, higher-power MI350/5X GPUs. The MI350P can be thought of as effectively half of a MI350X. To understand why, it helps to look at how the larger GPU is assembled.

The MI350X is a 3D-stacked chiplet design built on TSMC’s CoWoS, or Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate, packaging, with no single monolithic die. Eight accelerator complex dies, or XCDs, sit above two I/O dies, with four XCDs on each I/O die. AMD’s Infinity Fabric connects the chiplets, while eight HBM3E stacks provide the GPU’s memory. CoWoS describes the package-level integration; the compute-over-I/O arrangement is the design’s vertical, 3D-stacked component.

The MI350P takes one half of that arrangement: four XCDs, one I/O die, and four HBM3E stacks. Each XCD has 32 active compute units, giving the card 128 CUs compared with the MI350X’s 256. The memory resources are also halved: 144GB of HBM3E against 288GB, 4TB/s of bandwidth against 8TB/s, and 128MB of Infinity Cache against 256MB.

The 600W figure is a maximum, and AMD lets the card be configured down to 450W, which is where it ran in our 2U host. The H200 NVL matched it at 450W in the R770, but the RTX PRO 6000 ran at its full 600W in the XE7740, so the NVIDIA card had 150W more to work with in every comparison against it. The full-power results wait for a chassis that can cool a 600W passive card, and Dell’s XE7745 technical guide lists eight MI350Ps at 600W.
The other note: the single 12V-2×6 connector and the 10.5-inch, double-slot board, which is what lets the card go into the same risers that hold an RTX PRO 6000 or an H200 NVL today.

The table below sets the MI350P beside the three NVIDIA systems in our charts: the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, which shares its slot, its power range, and its PCIe 5.0 x16 host link; the H200 NVL, the Hopper card with the memory bandwidth to match it; and the GB300 DGX Station, a single Blackwell Ultra GPU paired with a Grace CPU over NVLink-C2C.

The rows to read first are memory capacity, where the MI350P’s 144GB is the largest of the three PCIe cards, 3GB above the H200 NVL and 48GB above the RTX PRO 6000; memory bandwidth, where its 4TB/s sits between the two; and the FP4 line, where AMD quotes a dense figure, and NVIDIA quotes sparse.

Against the RTX PRO 6000, the MI350P’s memory subsystem is the most immediate difference. It has 50 percent more GPU memory and roughly 2.5x the memory bandwidth. For a model that doesn’t fit comfortably within 96GB, the additional capacity could determine whether it runs on one GPU or needs to be distributed across several.

The RTX PRO 6000, however, serves a broader range of workloads, with hardware for graphics, ray tracing, and video alongside its AI capabilities. The choice weighs more than two peak compute figures; it also depends on what else the system needs to do.

The H200 NVL is the more direct comparison for the MI350P among high-memory PCIe accelerators; the larger Blackwell datacenter GPUs sit in a different class. Memory capacity is nearly identical at 144GB versus the H200’s 141GB, with both using HBM3E, and the H200 offers 20 percent more memory bandwidth at 4.8TB/s. The two also scale differently: all three PCIe cards connect to the host over PCIe, but the H200 NVL adds dedicated GPU-to-GPU connectivity through NVLink bridges connecting up to four GPUs.

The larger MI350X and MI355X were built to compete with Blackwell, but the MI350P cuts that hardware configuration in half. That brings it closer to the H200 NVL in memory attributes and in overall positioning. One place where the MI350P still distinguishes itself is native MXFP4 and MXFP6 support, which matters more as inference moves toward lower precision.

The smaller memory subsystem is another compromise, because AMD has not offset the reduction in HBM stacks with faster HBM3E, leaving the MI350P at 4TB/s of bandwidth and behind the H200 NVL on this metric. That can limit performance in memory-bandwidth-bound workloads, regardless of the available compute, as the memory bandwidth and long-prompt inference results later in the review show.

The DGX Station comparison runs the other way, because the GB300 Station carries a full B300 GPU with one HBM stack disabled, a datacenter-class chip on a datacenter power budget, while the MI350P is half of a datacenter-class chip fitted into the 600W envelope of a PCIe add-in card. AMD needs two or four MI350Ps to meet that single GPU, and on paper two of them do: 288GB and 8TB/s against the Station’s 252GB and 7.1TB/s. Those resources sit on two cards, though, and a workload spanning both exchanges data over PCIe peer-to-peer, which limits how much the second card adds.

The MI350P review unit is a Dell PowerEdge R7725 with two AMD EPYC 9555 processors (64 cores each), 1.5TB of DDR5-6400 across 24 DIMMs, and two MI350P cards set to 450W, the cap for a 2U server. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition cards (600W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge XE7740 that carries our four-card inference build, a single H200 NVL (450W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge R770 from our review, and the GB300 figures come from the ASUS ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3 DGX Station we reviewed in September.

The iDRAC inventory below shows how the two cards are seated. They sit in PCIe slots 2 and 7, both Gen5 x16 and both reporting healthy, and the device keys, 0-139-0 and 1-199-0, read to us as one card behind each EPYC socket, so tensor-parallel traffic between the two MI350Ps crosses the socket link on its way between root complexes. That is the layout a two-card deployment in a 2U server gets by default, and it is worth keeping in mind on the two-card results later.

The memory view shows the rest of the host: 24 DIMMs of 64GB DDR5-6400, dual rank, for 1,536GB in a server that tops out at 6TB, all with multi-bit ECC. The headroom matters for the GLM-5.2 run, where the MXFP4 checkpoint does not fit in two cards’ 288GB and vLLM offloads part of the expert weights to host memory.

To put the MI350P’s compute in context, we ran MAMF across the four systems. MAMF (Maximum Achievable Matmul FLOPS) is a practical performance metric designed to measure the realistic peak floating-point operations per second an accelerator reaches during matrix multiplication, a more useful benchmark than the theoretical peak FLOPS in the spec sheet. We sweep each system in BF16, FP8, and block-scaled FP4 and report the best sustained dense result per precision; the hatched bars multiply each PCIe card’s result by the card count used in the large-model serving runs and are calculated, with no measurement behind them.

At 450W, one MI350P reaches 580 TFLOPS in BF16, 1,120 in FP8, and 2,228 in FP4. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell follows at 419, 820, and 1,634, so the MI350P holds a 36 to 38 percent lead over the NVIDIA card at every precision while running 150W below it, with the widest gap in BF16 at 38.4 percent.

The H200 NVL’s 652 TFLOPS in BF16 and 1,205 in FP8 put it ahead of the MI350P on both, and it has no FP4 path. The GB300 DGX Station sits above all three PCIe cards at 1,924, 3,802, and 6,024, roughly 3.3x the MI350P at BF16 and 2.7x at FP4; two MI350Ps on paper close to 1,160 and 4,456, still short of the Station’s single GPU. The NVIDIA MAMF figures in this review come from our latest runs on each card and replace the results from our earlier testing.

Raw compute throughput is only useful if the accelerator can keep its execution units supplied with data. This matters most for inference, where token generation during the decode phase is limited more by memory bandwidth than by available FLOPS. The bandwidth test reads, writes, and copies GPU memory through compute kernels and the copy engine, showing the bandwidth available inside each GPU against its rated figure.

One MI350P reads its HBM3E at 3,291GB/s and writes at 3,204GB/s, about 80 percent of the 4TB/s rating, with copies at 1,276 to 1,283GB/s; a copy consumes bandwidth twice, once to read the source and again to write the destination. The RTX PRO 6000’s GDDR7 manages 1,540GB/s on reads and 1,483GB/s on writes, so the MI350P carries about 2.1x the usable bandwidth per card.

The H200 NVL’s 4,472GB/s read and 4,156GB/s write figures run 36 and 30 percent ahead of the MI350P, in line with its 4.8TB/s rating against 4TB/s, and the GB300 DGX Station reaches 6,869GB/s. Two MI350Ps measured together reach 6,529GB/s on reads, near the Station, but that bandwidth sits in two PCIe slots, and a model spanning both pays for every exchange over PCIe.

With the low-level tests covered, we move to LLM inference. Our vLLM online serving test drives an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a fixed number of concurrent streams and records output tokens per second across the run. We report two shapes: 512 tokens in and 512 out, which is chat-sized and decode-heavy, and 8,192 in and 1,024 out, which is RAG- and document-sized and leans on prefill. Concurrency doubles from one stream upward, and each chart stops at the highest concurrency at which every card in it completed. Every point is two requests per stream, so single-stream figures rest on two requests and carry more run-to-run variance than the higher-concurrency points.

Each model ran on the fewest cards that could hold it: one MI350P for everything through GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, and two for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash. The RTX PRO 6000 runs follow the same rule, which puts two RTX cards against one MI350P on MiniMax-M2.7 and four against two on MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2. Low-precision builds differ by vendor: AMD’s are MXFP4 through Quark, NVIDIA’s are NVFP4, and the FP4 pairings are labeled that way throughout. GPT-OSS ships as MXFP4 and runs the same weights on every card. The H200 NVFP4 builds are not included.

Read down the MI350P column, and the card count is the first thing 144GB gets you. Six of the ten models run on one MI350P, where the RTX PRO 6000’s 96GB needs a second card for MiniMax-M2.7, and the two MXFP4 checkpoints that stay on a pair of MI350Ps, MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2, need four RTX PRO 6000s. GLM-5.2 is the one that outgrows even 288GB, and vLLM offloads part of its expert weights to the R7725’s host memory for that run; the GB300 does the same with about 215GB of experts in Grace memory.

The MI350P figures for the single-card models were run October 27 on AMDGPU 31.60, ROCm 10.1.0, and vLLM 0.32.0. Dell’s validated combination is vLLM 0.27 with ROCm 10.0 and AMDGPU 31.5, and we went one step past it to the ROCm 10.1 release of October 5. The NVIDIA cards ran the vLLM 26.08 container on CUDA 13.4.1 throughout. The table lists the build behind each run.

The four two-card models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash, are reported from runs on ROCm 7.2.3. Our ROCm 10.1 passes on those models used CPU expert offload throughout and, on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, a speculative decoder the NVIDIA runs did not, which makes them a different test, so they are held for a clean pass on the current stack, and the tables label every MI350P row with its stack.

AMD’s preferred path for these models is its AIM containers; the Enterprise AI Suite 2.5 release of October 9 is validated on ROCm 10 and carries AIMs for GPT-OSS-120B, Llama 3.3 70B, and Gemma 3 27B, but AMD’s accelerator table lists an optimized MI350P profile only for Wan2.2 so far. Stock vLLM is therefore still the path an MI350P buyer takes today, and is what we measured.

There are 28 charts below, so here is the short version in two tables: output tokens per second for each model at the highest concurrency every card completed, with the chat-sized 512-in, 512-out workload first. The MI350P figures are one card at 450W unless the row says otherwise, with a column for the stack each row comes from; the GB300 DGX Station is a single B300.

Two results stand out in the chat table: the MI350P beats the RTX PRO 6000 on every FP8, BF16, and GPT-OSS model, by 35 to 65 percent at 128 streams, trails NVIDIA’s NVFP4 builds only at the top of the Llama and MiniMax-M2.7 curves, and roughly doubles the NVIDIA card at a single stream on Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral Small 24B, where 4TB/s of HBM3E does the work.

The H200 NVL, with 20 percent more bandwidth, stays 4 to 18 percent ahead on the dense FP8 and BF16 models at 128 streams and ties on Llama 3.1 8B FP8; on the two GPT-OSS models the order reverses, and the MI350P finishes 50 and 78 percent ahead.
The second table repeats the exercise on the 8,192-token prompts, where prefill dominates the run and the balance between compute and memory bandwidth shifts toward the NVIDIA cards.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the picture is mixed: the MI350P leads the RTX PRO 6000 on both GPT-OSS models at every stream count and on Mistral Small, splits Qwen3-Coder at 128 streams (24 percent ahead on BF16, 8 percent behind on FP8), and flattens by 16 streams on Llama and MiniMax-M2.7, where it finishes behind the NVIDIA card. Against the H200, it leads on GPT-OSS by 15 percent on the 120B model and 5 percent on the 20B at 128 streams and trails by 25 to 58 percent on the dense models.

On the largest models, where two MI350Ps face four RTX PRO 6000s, the NVIDIA set leads GLM-5.2 through 16 streams on the chat workload with 384GB of GDDR7 against 288GB of HBM3E, while on MiniMax-M3 all three configurations stay within 10 percent through eight streams before the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16. The single GB300 clears every PCIe configuration by a wide margin on anything that fits in its 252GB.

GLM-5.3 Flash was not run on the RTX PRO 6000, so the comparison is two MI350P cards against the single GB300 Station through 32 streams. On the chat workload, the MI350P pair starts behind, 45 against 353 output tokens per second at one stream, and crosses the Station at eight streams on its way to 1,462 at 32, against 828 for the Station. On the prefill-heavy workload the Station leads throughout, 1,219 against 760 at 32 streams, where the pair’s prefill has to cross PCIe between the two cards and the B300 does it all in one piece of HBM.

GLM-5.2 is the memory story in this set. The MXFP4 checkpoint spills past the two MI350P cards’ 288GB into host memory, so single-stream throughput is 2 output tokens per second on the pair against 9 for four RTX PRO 6000 cards holding the NVFP4 build in 384GB of GDDR7 and 35 for the Station, which offloads about 215GB of expert weights to Grace memory. The RTX quad leads through 16 streams on the chat workload; at 32 the MI350P pair reaches 59 against 40, and the Station reaches 139. On prefill-heavy prompts, neither PCIe configuration gets past single digits through 16 streams, against 87 for the Station.

Two MI350Ps hold the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M3 in 288GB; the NVIDIA side needs four RTX PRO 6000 cards. The three configurations run within 10 percent of each other through eight streams on the chat workload; the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16 (1,181 against 998 for the pair and 940 for the Station), and at 32 the MI350P pair reads 1,509 against 759 for the quad and 1,041 for the Station.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the MI350P pair leads at every point through eight streams, 524 against 444 for the quad, while the Station, which keeps a slice of this model’s experts in Grace memory, falls to 103.

With two cards on each side and the native FP8 checkpoint, the RTX PRO 6000 pair leads through eight streams on the chat workload and the MI350P pair takes over from 16, finishing at 1,081 against 829 at 32 streams; the single Station reaches 1,766 at the same point. The prefill-heavy run follows the same shape, the MI350P pair at 621 against 345 for the RTX pair at 32 streams and 954 for the Station.

One MI350P carries the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M2.7 against two RTX PRO 6000 cards on NVFP4. The single MI350P leads the pair at one stream (124 against 115), stays 8 to 20 percent ahead through 64 streams 1,486 against 1,339, then flattens at 1,524 at 128 and 1,557 at 256, while the RTX pair continues to 1,932 and 2,842; the Station reaches 4,793.
On the prefill-heavy workload, the MI350P holds at 304 to 331 output tokens per second from eight streams through 64, against 501 for the RTX pair and 1,744 for the Station.

articles.title: AMD EPYC 9006 Results Are Here and AMD Delivers a Knockout Part Deux
articles.summary: As far as server CPU launches go, today’s launch is remarkable on multiple levels. Besides taking a look at a wholly new server platform from AMD (socket and all), which would normally be a big event in and of itself, the server boom has turned the CPU development cycle on its head, and now it is a server CPU where we will see AMD’s latest CPU architecture. So along with our first benchmarks of Venice, today also marks our first chance to evaluate the Zen 6 CPU architecture that will be driving so many AMD products over the coming two years – everything ranging from server chips like Venice and Verano to consumer desktops, laptops, and more. There is a lot to unpack with today’s launch.
bodyEvidence: At long last, the day is here. Today, we finally get to share with you our first look at AMD’s EPYC “Venice” series, or the EPYC 9006 processors. Following AMD’s biennial CPU development roadmap, the highlight of the year for AMD’s CPU teams is the launch of the EPYC 9006 processors and the Zen 6 CPU architecture that underlies them. Amid an unprecedented explosion in demand for server CPUs for AI systems driving both host nodes and agentic workloads, AMD is in a commanding position, bringing to market a new generation of even more powerful server hardware right when the industry needs it most. All the while, AMD has ambitions of becoming the undisputed market leader for server CPUs, ambitions that Venice seems primed to help AMD reach.

As far as server CPU launches go, today’s launch is remarkable on multiple levels. Besides taking a look at a wholly new server platform from AMD (socket and all), which would normally be a big event in and of itself, the server boom has turned the CPU development cycle on its head, and now it is a server CPU where we will see AMD’s latest CPU architecture. So along with our first benchmarks of Venice, today also marks our first chance to evaluate the Zen 6 CPU architecture that will be driving so many AMD products over the coming two years – everything ranging from server chips like Venice and Verano to consumer desktops, laptops, and more. There is a lot to unpack with today’s launch.

With so much to do and so little time to do it all, we are going to have a lot more content to follow. But to get things started, for today’s launch piece we are going to run the flagship EPYC 9996 through not only our agentic-workload-focused AgentSTH V7 benchmark suite, but we are also including bits and pieces of what is essentially a preview of 2027’s AgentSTH V8. For some context, we are going back roughly a decade in server architectures to not just blindly pick up benchmark suites, but to profile workloads on dozens of platforms for inclusion in the suite.

We have lots of numbers for this one and some neat comparison points. The headline feature is that we now get up to 256 cores per socket, a new PCIe Gen6 I/O subsystem, and more than twice the memory bandwidth to go along with a revised Zen 6 microarchitecture and SoC design. AMD is also splitting its lineup into multiple families for different applications with two primary sockets, a return of the -X high-cache parts with Venice-X, and the LPDDR5X Verano. The new series covers a lot more and is by far the most ambitious innovation in the EPYC line since the switch to an I/O die, which allowed the EPYC 7002 to deliver a knockout . This is the Knockout Part Deux.

I also wanted to recognize Ryan, Sam, and Vic for helping us turn this around quickly. We will have Ryan cover the Zen 6/6c microarchitecture and SoC portion before I take back over on performance. Regular STH readers may have noticed this, but many of our pieces are much longer than they used to be, and doing these reviews has become a team effort.

Over the summer, AMD held a proper unveiling for its EPYC 9006 “Venice” server CPU platform at the company’s annual Advancing AI event. In what has become AMD’s marquee event of the year – and a reflection of the importance of server parts to their bottom line – the company laid out an aggressive plan for 2026 and beyond. Spearheaded by the Venice CPU platform, AMD has ambitions to deliver not only its most powerful and most capable server platform to date, but to iterate on that over the next year or so to deliver a broad portfolio of server chips that covers everything from rank-and-file servers to mighty HPC systems, and of course lots of AI nodes.

Now in its sixth generation of Zen-architecture server chips, Venice is in some respects AMD’s most aggressive design yet. AMD is making heavier use of chiplets than ever before, and the company is now relying on advanced packaging techniques to tie them all together. This has allowed AMD to fully leverage TSMC’s N2 (2nm) process node, their first GAAFET-based node, to the best of their abilities, tapping it to not only devote more transistors than ever to the Zen CPU cores to boost their performance, but to pack in more CPU cores than ever before.

For high-throughput workloads, the highlight of Venice is that there are now up to 256 CPU cores in a single socket, a 33% improvement over EPYC 9005 “Turin” only a generation ago, and with 20% higher IPC and higher clock speeds on top of that. Meanwhile, for workloads where single-threaded performance and latency are more critical, AMD is bringing the 5.3GHz EPYC 9686F to market to double down on Zen 6’s IPC improvements with the highest clock speeds yet for an EPYC server chip.

AMD is keen to tap into the agentic era of computing. And there are a lot of improvements to Venice and the Zen 6 CPU architecture that are going to help them get there. But do not underestimate the chip in other areas, either. AMD has invested in features such as PCIe Gen6, new virtualization and security features, and it has even picked up a software engineering firm in recent months to develop software to replace DRAM with flash memory. AI is certainly the highlight of the Venice story, but it is not the only story.

With any luck, AMD expects that over the next 12 months they will finally reach the point where they capture leadership of the server CPU market. As we saw with AMD’s earnings last week , the company’s data center division is already projecting that its revenues will surpass Intel’s in Q4 of this year. Meanwhile, AMD already holds 46% of the x86 server CPU revenue share, and the company seems confident that Venice will push it above 50% for the first time.

Alongside its initial summer announcement of the EPYC 9006 lineup, AMD also published the complete specifications for its full stack of Venice chip SKUs . This was for both the high-end SP7 platform launching today, as well as the more restrained SP8 platform that is launching early next year.

As it turns out, AMD was sandbagging things a bit. Whereas their flagship high-frequency chip, the EPYC 9686F, was originally announced to ship with a peak frequency of 5.0GHz, that is no longer the case.
Instead, the 9686F is now a 5.3GHz chip. Making this a notable improvement just ahead of the launch of the hardware, and admittedly a bit of a point of pride (or at least bragging rights) for AMD.

In talking with AMD, the company tells us that they have found that the final silicon for their Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCDs has turned out even better than the company was expecting. Consequently, their earlier SKU stack was a bit conservative with clockspeeds, and they can do a bit better than 5.0GHz – ultimately allowing the fastest Venice to clock higher than the fastest Turin after all.

In fact, almost the entire SP7 lineup has received a clockspeed bump. Outside of the flagship EPYC 9996, every other chip in the stack has seen its max boost clockspeeds revised upwards. Now there is not a single chip with a peak clockspeed lower than 4.1GHz (Zen 6c parts), while all of the high-frequency Zen 6 parts now top out at 5.3GHz. Base clockspeeds have been revised upwards as well, with most chips picking up around 100MHz compared to AMD’s preliminary specifications.
So here is what the final, shipping SP7 chip stack looks like.

AMD has also used this opportunity to sneak in one last chip SKU ahead of today’s launch. The EPYC 9956 has been added to the product stack; this is a lower clocked version of AMD’s biggest 256 core configuration, with a similarly reduced TDP of 400 Watts. So AMD’s customers now have a couple of options if they want a high throughput 256 core part.

articles.title: Supermicro Super AI Station Review: The AI Server That Doubles as a Workstation
articles.summary: Today we are taking a look at our latest DGX Station system with Supermicro’s Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC). By squeezing in as much compute hardware as a 1.6kW power supply can sustain, NVIDIA and its partners are positioning these systems as the ultimate desk-side AI boxes for local AI work.
bodyEvidence: With several partners in its DGX Station initiative, NVIDIA’s project to bring its server-grade Grace Blackwell GB300 hardware to desktop workstations has no shortage of hardware suppliers. Or system designs, for that matter. Of all of these, Supermicro is a clear frontrunner for the most interesting workstation, thanks to its unique, convertible design.

Today we are taking a look at our latest DGX Station system with Supermicro’s Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC). By squeezing in as much compute hardware as a 1.6kW power supply can sustain, NVIDIA and its partners are positioning these systems as the ultimate desk-side AI boxes for local AI work.

Meanwhile, every DGX Station vendor is putting their own spin on how a GB300 desktop should be built, and Supermicro is no different. For Supermicro, that means taking the “server at your desk” motif a little more literally than most, by developing a system that can either be set up as a full-size desktop tower or placed in a rack as a 5U system. It is, without a doubt, quintessentially Supermicro and a great example of how the company has applied its server expertise to the workstation market. It also makes a lot of sense given what we have learned with the networking on these systems.
Without further ado, let us dive right in.

The first time you see Supermicro’s Super AI Server, it is immediately obvious that it is different from the full-tower PCs other DGX Station vendors offer. For their own DGX Station system, Supermicro has done the most Supermicro thing possible by putting the system inside of a convertible chassis. This system can be set up as a desktop workstation, or it can be put on rails and rack-mounted as a 5U server.

That kind of convertible design has a huge impact on the system design, as we will see. Both the system’s form factor and internal layout have been optimized to fulfill both roles, which at times makes this a very different system from other DGX Station systems.

One immediate impact of that design is that the Super AI Station is a bit shorter and much deeper than a typical PC tower workstation. At 455mm tall, the Super AI Station is skinny enough to fit between a pair of rack posts. The trade-off is that it is 701mm (or nearly 28 inches) long.

With 1600 watts of hardware to cool, the Super AI Station is best described as a high-airflow system. Almost every square millimeter of space on the front of the system is dedicated to drawing in air to cool the system.

The sole exception to that is a small front I/O panel, which, despite the heavy airflow emphasis, marks the first time we have seen an actual front I/O panel on a DGX Station. Supermicro’s server roots make themselves apparent here once again, as the port collection is a simple pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports. Compared with other systems, we have seen other vendors put 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C ports here, underscoring the server roots of this design once more. The ports themselves are adequately labeled, but it feels a bit more like a server in this respect.

Otherwise, the front I/O panel is rounded out with the power button, a smaller reset button, and finally a drive activity LED. The system status LED is embedded in the power button and can illuminate red or blue, depending on the system status.
To the left of the front I/O panel is a locked cage, which hides the system’s service tag information. This area could also theoretically house front panel storage expansion.

As for the sides of the Super AI Station, both sides are unremarkable. Unlike Supermicro’s fun demo unit back at Computex , the production hardware does not come with a plexiglass window. If you want to see inside, you will have to take the side panels off. Since the system is convertible, Supermicro doesn’t rely on the sides for significant ventilation, so these panels are little more than simple steel sheets.

Flipping over to the rear of the system, we finally get a better idea of just how different the Super AI Station is from more standard workstations: this is not a standard EEB/E-ATX chassis. The power supply is on its own side of the system, there is an obvious coolant tank, and, though not obvious in this shot, the motherboard is installed upside-down. The PCIe slot brackets are at the top of the system.
Because NVIDIA provides the motherboards for all these DGX Station systems, the port layout is standardized, so Supermicro’s matches the other vendors.

Starting on the left, the system’s two QSFP112 ports are fed by the powerful NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC. Each port offers 400Gbps networking and is the primary way the system connects to high-speed storage and/or other DGX Station-based systems. We have shown that these systems can push 800Gbps through the NIC in certain circumstances. The ConnectX-8 SuperNIC driving these ports does a lot of heavy lifting beyond networking, and the capabilities and limitations of these QSFP ports are somewhat complex as a result (more on this in a bit). Meanwhile, there is a grate above the QSFP cages to allow for a bit more airflow for cooling.

For more mundane networking use cases, the system also has a pair of RJ45 Ethernet jacks. The left 1G port connects to the BMC and is for system management. OpenBMC handles management via an HTML5 iKVM. The RJ45 jack on the right side is a 10Gb Ethernet port powered by Marvell’s tried-and-true 10GbE controller. The system topology is fascinating. Marvell’s 10Gbase-T controller is attached to the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC’s built-in PCIe switch, then to the CPU. It does not connect directly to the CPU.

Below are the remaining USB ports. These four ports all run at 10Gbps, making these the fastest USB ports on the system. This also means that since NVIDIA did not include USB-C ports in its motherboard design, you will not find any USB-C ports on the Super AI Station.
To the right, we have a trio of audio jacks for two-channel audio out, plus separate mic and line-in jacks.

At the end of the rear I/O panel, two more ports connect to the BMC. On the left is a serial UART in a micro-USB form factor. To the right is a Mini DisplayPort output from the BMC for system management and configuration. DGX Station systems do not have a true integrated display GPU (Blackwell Ultra is more of a compute accelerator), so the BMC provides the only out-of-the-box graphics output. For a full-featured graphics solution, you can pair DGX Station systems with a compatible NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell video card. In this case, Supermicro has included an RTX PRO 2000 Blackwell card.

Notably, no port is labeled on the rear of the system. Supermicro has seemingly opted not to print anything on its I/O shield, at least in this example. For a server, this is par for the course, but as the Super AI Station is meant to double as a workstation, it would have been nice to see. We have an early system, so sometimes those early systems miss details like that.

Like all DGX Station systems, the Super AI Station is liquid-cooled. Supermicro’s design makes this obvious. The company uses an externally accessible coolant tank mounted toward the top of the system. Because the system comes completely pre-built, the Super AI Station is designed for minimal maintenance, so the externally accessible tank seems like a holdover from data center systems that can require more active maintenance. Regardless, if the system starts running low on coolant, the liquid level indicator makes it easy to see, and there are ports for filling and draining the system.

Elsewhere, near the bottom of the system, we have the Super AI Station’s 1600 Watt power supply. While the wattage is standardized across DGX Station systems, the actual power supply model is not. This benefits Supermicro, as theirs is the first DGX Station system to cross our labs with an 80 Plus Titanium-rated power supply, one step higher than the Platinum units we have seen in other systems.

Because Supermicro put all of their front I/O and buttons on the front of the system, there is no need for the top of the system to be anything special. Coupled with the fact that it has no ventilation here, since that would not work in a rackmount scenario, Supermicro is keeping things simple on top. This top can be popped off to expose mounting points for rackmount rails.
The bottom, for that matter. Here it is much more obvious, even in a workstation configuration, that this chassis can be rack-mounted, as you can easily see where the rails would go.
This also means that for workstation mode, the chassis needs a pair of feet attached to properly support the system and its copious 88lb weight.
That wraps things up for our outside look at the Super AI Station. For the rest of the story, let us dive into the system’s chassis, where this gets very different.

bodyEvidence: Seagate announced that its Mozaic hard drives built on heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) and configured for shingled magnetic recording (SMR) have been added to Broadcom’s approved vendor list for its host bus adapters, which Seagate calls the first and only SMR drives on the list. Microsoft Azure Storage has qualified the Broadcom HBA with Seagate HAMR plus SMR drives for its fleet, which gives the pairing a hyperscale proof point. The practical effect is that a buyer can order the highest-capacity Seagate drives and a Broadcom controller as a supported combination without doing the interoperability work themselves.

Seagate’s announcement names no part numbers, but Broadcom’s compatibility report for the eHBA 96xx family does. The new SMR section lists two Seagate SATA 6Gb/s models, the 32TB ST32000NM001F on firmware SR05 and the 36TB ST36000NM001M on firmware SR01, both qualified at Broadcom firmware phase MR8.17 with 512-byte logical sectors, against the eHBA 9620-16i, 9600-24i, and 9600-16i Tri-Mode adapters. Those are the SMR versions of the Exos M line on the Mozaic 3+ platform, the 3TB-per-platter HAMR design that Seagate took to 36TB with SMR.

The same report, updated the same day, also carries an SMR page for Western Digital, listing 17 Ultrastar DC HC690 models at Broadcom firmware phase MR8.18. Seagate’s drives sit one firmware phase earlier, which supports the “first” in Seagate’s claim, but Broadcom’s list no longer supports “only,” and buyers comparing the two SMR camps can now do it on the same adapter. Both lists are SATA only; no SAS SMR models appear for either vendor.

SMR overlaps adjacent tracks to raise capacity, which turns the drive into a zoned device: data is written sequentially inside zones, and the host or the drive has to manage the rewrites. Host-managed SMR drives in particular do not behave like conventional disks at the SCSI and ATA command level, and an HBA or RAID stack that does not pass the zone commands through cleanly will refuse the drive or corrupt it.

That is why SMR has lived almost entirely inside hyperscalers that write the host software themselves. When we tested the host-managed Exos X26z , Windows did not see the drive at all, a Supermicro server’s SAS bays did not detect it under Ubuntu, and it only appeared on a direct SATA cable with a zoned btrfs file system on top.

An AVL entry means Broadcom has run the drive through its interoperability suite on the named adapters and firmware, and will support the combination. Broadcom describes the HBA’s role as the communication path that lets large numbers of drives be connected, addressed, and managed by the host, and frames the SMR qualification as a path for more customers to integrate and manage high-capacity drive fleets. For an enterprise or a second-tier cloud that wants Azure-class density on a standard server, that support ticket is the difference between an SMR tier being a project and being a purchase.

Microsoft’s Azure Memory and Storage Center of Excellence completed the qualification of the Broadcom HBA with Seagate’s HAMR plus SMR drives. “At hyperscale, storage infrastructure has to meet demanding requirements for interoperability, manageability and infrastructure efficiency at scale,” said Pablo Ziperovich, general manager, Azure Memory and Storage Center of Excellence at Microsoft. “Microsoft Azure’s joint validation and qualification of Seagate and Broadcom’s SMR configuration demonstrates how these technologies can work together across large data center deployments, enabling greater storage density at a similar cost and power envelope.”

The cost and power clause is the business case, because the 36TB SMR drive fits the same 3.5-inch bay as the 30TB and 32TB CMR Exos M, so a rack of them adds capacity without adding slots or controllers, and Microsoft’s statement puts the cost and power envelope as similar. Seagate has not published pricing for the SMR models.

“High-capacity storage innovation delivers the greatest value when customers put that capacity to work efficiently,” said Jason Feist, Senior Vice President, Cloud Business at Seagate. “By pairing Seagate HAMR + SMR storage technology with Broadcom’s connectivity infrastructure, we’re helping make high-capacity SMR storage more accessible and easier to deploy as AI and cloud data demands grow.”

articles.title: Oracle Acceleron Adds Front-End RDMA, an NCCL and RCCL Plugin for Multiplanar Failover, and 3x NVMe Block Storage Performance on OCI
articles.summary: “AI infrastructure can be unforgiving when it comes to network friction,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “When thousands of accelerators are working together, one congested or failed path can have consequences far beyond a single connection. With Oracle Acceleron, we are building a network that can respond by rerouting traffic, recovering from failures, and helping customers scale securely.”
bodyEvidence: Oracle announced a second round of Oracle Acceleron capabilities at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, a year after the networking suite first bundled dedicated fabrics, multiplanar networking, SmartNICs, and direct data paths for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The new pieces are RDMA on OCI’s shared front-end network, NVMe block storage attachments across Acceleron bare metal and VM shapes that Oracle rates at up to 3x the block performance, a collective communications plugin that moves failover and load balancing into the NCCL and RCCL layer, and multiplanar networking extended to front-end traffic.

“AI infrastructure can be unforgiving when it comes to network friction,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “When thousands of accelerators are working together, one congested or failed path can have consequences far beyond a single connection. With Oracle Acceleron, we are building a network that can respond by rerouting traffic, recovering from failures, and helping customers scale securely.”

OCI’s front-end network carries Oracle Database, customer compute, block and object storage, SaaS and OCI services, backbone links, internet access, and on-premises connectivity on the same fabric, which is why RDMA has historically stayed on dedicated back-end cluster networks. The Oracle Acceleron High-Performance Fabric puts RDMA on that shared front end for inference, storage, and HPC traffic, and Oracle says it supports every queue pair type and verb, so existing RDMA applications run without changes. The company also uses the front-end links to connect separate GPU clusters while the back-end fabrics handle training inside each cluster.

The storage half is the expanded NVMe block storage attachment options across the new Acceleron bare metal and VM shapes, which Oracle says improve NVMe block storage performance by up to 3x for AI, database, and other data-intensive workloads. Oracle has not published the baseline configuration, the workload, or whether the figure is throughput, IOPS, or latency, and we did not run or audit it. The release carries Oracle’s standard future product disclaimer and gives no availability dates for any of the new capabilities.

Sharing a front end between RDMA and TCP is a congestion-control problem, since RDMA transports typically use rate-based control and TCP uses window-based control, and one loop can starve the other. Oracle’s answer lives in the Acceleron SmartNIC. Hierarchical token buckets track bandwidth for RDMA and non-RDMA classes under a shared parent bucket, and as tokens run low the NIC probabilistically marks ECN-capable packets or drops the rest, which produces a gradual congestion signal and also heads off incast at the top-of-rack link. Either class can borrow unused bandwidth from the other.

For congestion inside the fabric, the SmartNIC runs One-Way-Delay Congestion Control, measuring forward-path delay so that a congested reverse path does not trigger a false signal. When it sees elevated delay on a flow, it probes three alternate paths and moves the flow if one is better; if none is, it falls back to ECN marking or drops. Oracle describes the design as needing minimal QoS support from the switches while keeping standard kernel and CPU bypass on the hosts.

OCI’s back-end Multiplanar Network connects multi-port NICs to several disjoint fabrics so a training job has n-way redundancy, but using those planes has required NIC-level functionality that is not always available. The Oracle Collective Communications Library plugin removes that dependency. It is a CCL network plugin that natively supports the NVIDIA NCCL and AMD RCCL plugin interfaces, the layer frameworks use to turn collective operations into NIC transfers, and it carries failover, recovery, and congestion-aware load balancing inside the plugin, independent of NIC firmware and topology.

In operation, OCCL distributes collective traffic across multiple standard Reliable Connection queue pairs, sends more over the pairs showing higher throughput, and moves traffic off congested paths at the message and chunk level. When a port or a whole NIC fails, it steers the collective to another port or NIC so the job continues without a restart. Oracle’s framing is that this is simpler than routing controllers that pick fabric paths and watch for changes, and it works on single-plane and multi-plane networks alike. The same multiplanar path selection and failover now reaches front-end RDMA traffic through what Oracle calls Transparent Front-End Multiplanar Networking.

The same networking update covered two items outside Acceleron. OCI Global CDN Connect provides direct connections between OCI Object Storage and Cloudflare, Fastly, Netskrt, and Mainstreaming, with zero OCI egress charges on eligible cache fetches in supported regions, and Oracle has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with F5 for a planned OCI App Defense web application and API protection service.

Dell Managed Detection and Response for Identity, also available now, adds 24×7 monitoring and response for suspicious authentication activity, compromised accounts, and privilege misuse; when the service detects defined attack patterns, Dell’s team can initiate automated response actions to contain the threat.

The PowerProtect AI Assistant gains an expanded conversational interface for assets, tasks, restores, and reporting. Proactive daily briefs surface potential risks before they escalate, and a human-in-the-loop approval workflow lets teams review and approve actions before they are taken. Those expanded capabilities are available now.

bodyEvidence: Smartbird and WEKA have announced a partnership that puts WEKA NeuralMesh inside Smartbird’s dedicated AI clusters, sold as a managed service for enterprise AI workloads. Smartbird designs, builds, and operates each cluster for a single customer’s workloads, on-premises or in a dedicated colocation facility, and the companies describe the result as sovereign by design, with customer data staying in a customer-controlled environment and production-ready from day one. The agreement is the first in a planned network of Smartbird infrastructure partnerships.

Smartbird is the company formerly known as Allbirds. Allbirds sold its footwear brand and assets, changed its name to Smartbird, Inc. in June, kept the NASDAQ listing under the BIRD ticker, and named Dr. Nadia Carlsten, previously CEO of GPU compute provider DCAI, as president and CEO. Its first clusters were still being designed at the time of the rename, with data center sites under development in the U.S. and Europe, which makes the WEKA deal the first look at what the stack will contain.

NeuralMesh supplies the data and memory layer. The companies say GPUs stay continuously supplied with data at throughput reaching hundreds of gigabytes per second, but the companies have not identified the hardware configurations, software versions, or test conditions behind that figure. For inference and continuously running agentic applications, the companies say the combined platform expands GPU memory capacity, shortens time to first token, and reduces recomputation, which they tie to lower token costs.

WEKA’s answer to those three in NeuralMesh is Augmented Memory Grid , the KV cache tier that extends GPU memory into NeuralMesh storage, and WEKA’s figures for it are up to 1000x more GPU memory capacity, up to 20x faster time to first token, and 10x more concurrent users on the same GPUs, which it attributes to production benchmarks. Those are WEKA’s numbers for NeuralMesh in general; the Smartbird announcement does not say which NeuralMesh components the clusters use and carries no measured GPU utilization, power, or cost-per-token results for them.

“Enterprises don’t want to assemble AI infrastructure from individual parts. They want a complete solution that works, operated by people who have done this before,” said Dr. Nadia Carlsten, president and CEO of Smartbird. “Every Smartbird AI cluster is designed around the customer’s specific requirements, whether they’re a bank, a hospital, a manufacturer, or a government agency. By incorporating WEKA NeuralMesh, Smartbird gives customers a data and memory layer proven to perform at scale.”

“Agentic AI is unforgiving: idle GPUs and stalled pipelines land straight on the P&L statement. Enterprises have been told the fix is a tradeoff, performance or sovereignty, but that was always a failure of infrastructure, not a law of physics,” said Liran Zvibel, co-founder and CEO at WEKA. “WEKA NeuralMesh ends the tradeoff. Smartbird delivers it as dedicated clusters customers don’t have to build or operate. Together, we’re giving regulated industries production AI that runs at full speed, on infrastructure only they touch, with more output per GPU, per watt and per dollar.”

Smartbird operates the full stack, covering facilities, compute, networking, data infrastructure, and data orchestration, so the customer has one accountable partner and does not integrate vendors or track multiple hardware release cycles. Each cluster is mapped one-to-one to its customer, and the companies say the fully dedicated footprint provides the isolation, encryption, and auditability that government, healthcare, and financial services workloads require. The companies have not named deployment jurisdictions, encryption implementation, or compliance certifications.

Although the companies describe the platform as production-ready from day one, there is no general availability date, no named customer, and Smartbird’s sites were still under development as of the June rename. NeuralMesh itself is the shipping product in the pair: WEKA took it to general availability in March and moved it to multi-tenant NeuralMesh 6 in July, with a parallel deal that puts it under Andromeda’s 50-plus GPU providers .

articles.title: NVIDIA Minerva Brings AIOps to AI Factories Through Dell, Lenovo, and Supermicro
articles.summary: The problem Minerva targets is one every large cluster operator knows: thousands of GPUs on a high-speed fabric behave as one machine, so a single part running out of spec drags the whole job with it. NVIDIA’s examples are a GPU running hotter than its neighbors and an NVMe drive losing performance under load, the kind of data signal that today sits in a networking tool, a compute tool, and an ML team’s dashboard, each with a separate view of the same cluster.
bodyEvidence: NVIDIA announced Minerva at GTC Berlin, an AIOps platform that pulls telemetry from GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers, and the AI workloads running on them, then applies machine learning to find a degrading component before it slows a training job. Dell Technologies, Lenovo, and Supermicro will offer it in their AI factory operations portfolios, IREN is already running it, and IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI, Tesla, Aolani, and Bitdeer AI plan to deploy it. NVIDIA has not published pricing or a general availability date.

The problem Minerva targets is one every large cluster operator knows: thousands of GPUs on a high-speed fabric behave as one machine, so a single part running out of spec drags the whole job with it. NVIDIA’s examples are a GPU running hotter than its neighbors and an NVMe drive losing performance under load, the kind of data signal that today sits in a networking tool, a compute tool, and an ML team’s dashboard, each with a separate view of the same cluster.

Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that maps GPUs, SuperNICs, switches, cables, and the jobs scheduled onto them, then analyzes what NVIDIA describes as billions of data points per hour with supervised and unsupervised machine learning. The models learn normal behavior for the factory, flag anomalies they have not seen before, predict failures that are developing, and correlate related events using the topology, so a slow training job can be traced to the component responsible across factories NVIDIA sizes at hundreds of thousands of GPUs.

The output is organized as incidents, with related events grouped into a single item and a likely root cause attached, which NVIDIA says replaces a flood of alerts with one actionable item. A built-in assistant answers natural-language questions against the live telemetry and recommends a fix, and the platform connects to external agentic tools. Operators choose whether a person applies the remediation or whether Minerva hands it to automation through infrastructure APIs and external systems.

NVIDIA frames the payoff as AI factory yield, which it measures in GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime, and token production. The claimed results are longer intervals between interruptions, faster repairs, and fewer alerts to triage, with the operations team moving from reactive to proactive maintenance. Those are vendor claims without figures attached; NVIDIA has not published mean-time-to-repair or uptime numbers for Minerva.

NVIDIA already sells operations software for its reference designs. Mission Control , introduced in March 2025, handles cluster provisioning through Base Command Manager, workload management through Run:ai, telemetry, and autonomous job recovery for DGX SuperPOD systems. The same week as Minerva, NVIDIA put three open source DSX OS components into developer preview for AI factory lifecycle management: Config Manager for network configuration, Rack Management Service for rack-level power, inventory, firmware, and switch management, and Cluster Readiness Engine for validating GPU clusters with distributed workloads.

The scale of the problem Minerva is aimed at was on display in Meta’s Prometheus write-up last week. Meta runs each NVL72 domain as a 64-GPU slice with the other eight GPUs held as in-rack spares, keeps about 2 percent of racks in reserve, and quarantines every repaired system until it passes validation. A year of root-cause work with NVIDIA engineers on site cut interruptions by 99 percent and pushed the mean time between interruptions past 54,000 GPU hours, with a target of 100,000.

That is a hyperscaler running a purpose-built telemetry pipeline and a joint triage team with NVIDIA. Minerva looks like a packaged version of that discipline, something closer to out of the box for an enterprise or neocloud that wants hyperscaler-grade visibility into GPU, fabric, and storage health, and the spare-and-restart workflow that goes with it, delivered through the same OEMs that sell it the racks.

NVIDIA has not said how Minerva relates to Mission Control or DSX OS, whether it ships as software, an appliance, or a hosted service, or what the OEM packaging from Dell, Lenovo, and Supermicro will look like. The product’s documentation page directs customers to their NVIDIA account team for the user guide. The customer reference is IREN, which NVIDIA says is using Minerva to optimize its AI factories today.

“NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them,” said Denis Skrinnikoff, chief technology officer of IREN, who credited it with shifting the team’s time toward proactive maintenance.

For the storage side of the house, the interesting claim is that drive behavior under load is an input alongside GPU and fabric telemetry, since an NVMe device that is slowing down rarely shows up in GPU utilization until a checkpoint or data-loading stage stalls. How deep that storage telemetry goes, and which OEM and array platforms feed it, is the detail that will be interesting to dive into as we see this solution come to market.

bodyEvidence: NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin announcements today span containerized Vera Rubin infrastructure, a 2.5x expansion of its substrate supply, and software for AI factory power management and agent security, along with telecom, autonomous vehicle, robotics, and healthcare programs. The headline number is a deployment target: NVIDIA says its new DSX POD reference design cuts an AI factory’s deployment at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner-built systems due in early 2027.

NVIDIA DSX POD combines Vera Rubin compute with networking, cabling, rack-level power, and liquid cooling in factory-built containers. Partners complete rack-to-rack cabling, wiring, piping, and functional validation before shipment, so a delivered container connects to prepared power, cooling, and networking at the site. NVIDIA attributes the shorter window to finishing integration and testing at the manufacturing facility; the 14-day figure assumes a prepared site and leaves out the time to build the supporting facility.

Partners targeting worldwide delivery in early 2027 are Anduril, Armada, Bull, Crusoe, DayOne, Dell Technologies, Delta, Eaton, Foxconn (Ingrasys), GIGABYTE, HPE, Lenovo, Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Schneider Electric, Vertiv, and Wistron. Dell’s version , the Dell Modular Data Center with NVIDIA DSX POD, was announced this morning with the same early 2027 timing. NVIDIA has not published per-POD capacity, rack counts, or pricing.

NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. A multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to IBIDEN supports expansion of IBIDEN’s Ono Plant in Japan to three times its current capacity, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in Q1 2028. Samsung Electro-Mechanics joins NVIDIA’s substrate supply chain with capacity from its existing South Korean operations plus facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan.

NVIDIA is also supporting Unimicron’s KF substrate expansion in Taiwan through a capacity reservation agreement, with capacity arriving from Q2 2027 and full capacity by mid-2028. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA.

NVIDIA and Amkor plan to increase interposer wafer capacity in South Korea by more than 300 percent by the end of 2028. NVIDIA expects its total semiconductor testing capacity to double from 2026 to 2027 through expansion in the U.S., Taiwan, and Singapore; a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to King Yuan Electronics (KYEC) funds new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027, and expanded Singapore testing operations target high-volume production in February 2027.

For co-packaged optics, NVIDIA and Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) plan to expand Taiwanese optical-engine manufacturing capacity by 15x by mid-2027, then double it again by the end of 2028. Every figure in this section is a planned capacity target, and NVIDIA gives no current baseline volumes.

NVIDIA DSX is the full-stack reference architecture that combines compute, networking, storage, software, power, and cooling. Its software components are DSX MaxLPS for dynamic power allocation within a provisioned budget, DSX Flex for coordinating workload power with grid conditions, DSX Sim for simulation, DSX OS for infrastructure management, and DSX Exchange for connecting computing and facility systems.

Vera Rubin infrastructure supports 100 percent liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45 degrees Celsius, and the DSX reference designs connect it to closed-loop, dry-cooler heat rejection. NVIDIA says those designs can cut facility cooling water consumption to near zero, with local climate deciding whether supplemental mechanical cooling is needed in the hottest periods. At a 2-gigawatt scale, NVIDIA estimates savings of 54 million liters of water per day against conventional cooling-tower systems.

NVIDIA says DSX MaxLPS can deliver the same token output using up to 30 percent less power. In a Lambda proof of concept on HGX B200 systems, the company reports 24 percent higher cluster token throughput and 19 percent more GPU capacity within a fixed power budget, and an Nscale evaluation across four GB300 NVL72 racks in Iceland reports 49 percent higher inference throughput and 37 percent more managed GPU capacity within the same 264-kilowatt provisioned budget. These are vendor results, and we did not run or audit them.

DSX Flex coordinates workload demand with utility conditions, demand-response events, energy prices, onsite generation, and storage. In an early trial with Emerald AI, EPRI, Nebius, the U.K. National Grid, and NVIDIA, a Blackwell Ultra cluster reduced power draw by up to 40 percent during simulated grid events while critical workloads kept running.

NVIDIA’s new SimReady Central Library provides validated power and cooling equipment assets for DSX digital twins. Nscale uses DSX Sim at facilities in Portugal and Iceland, and Schneider Electric, AVEVA, Siemens, Dassault Systèmes, Vertiv, ABB, PTC, and Procore are contributing equipment models, simulation, or construction workflows; ABB’s work also covers 800 VDC development through its Infinitus Direct Current portfolio.

Three DSX OS components enter developer preview: NVIDIA Config Manager for network configuration, NVIDIA Rack Management Service for rack-level power, inventory, firmware, and switch management, and NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine for distributed validation and node-level fault isolation. They join NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller, NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime, and NVSentinel.

On the facility side, Trane Technologies has published seven thermal management reference designs, three of them 250-megawatt DSX-based cooling designs. Trane’s LiquidStack GigaModular and Vertiv’s 2.3-megawatt CoolChip coolant distribution units have qualified in their DSX Ready categories, and Hitachi Energy’s battery energy storage system has earned DSX Ready BESS qualification.

NVIDIA and Nokia are moving platforms that run radio access network software and AI services on shared accelerated infrastructure toward commercial service. NVIDIA says nearly 20 operators have publicly announced AI-RAN collaborations using Nokia anyRAN software and NVIDIA Aerial RAN Computer (ARC).

T-Mobile completed what NVIDIA describes as the world’s first AI-RAN call on a commercial network, in Bellevue, Washington, using commercial ARC servers, Nokia’s CUDA-accelerated RAN software, massive MIMO radios, an existing 5G Standalone core, and a commercial smartphone. Elisa ran voice, mobile data, and video analytics at the same time on ARC in an over-the-air 5G field environment, which NVIDIA says clears the way for commercial AI-RAN services in 2027. BT plans live trials in Birmingham in 2027, Deutsche Telekom plans field trials after validating the platform in Bonn and Oulu, and Orange is testing Nokia 5G software on ARC for spectral efficiency and edge services.

Two new ARC configurations, MGX 2U and MGX 4U, use NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs and will offer x86 or NVIDIA Vera CPU options. Dell Technologies, QCT, and Supermicro will offer ARC-ready servers; NVIDIA gives no ship date for either configuration.

Deutsche Telekom is expanding its Industrial AI Cloud and demonstrating robotics workloads distributed across onboard, edge, and central infrastructure. Orange is deploying ARC for voice applications on Nemotron Speech, and Elisa has deployed an ARC-based enterprise voice assistant. NVIDIA also lists new infrastructure projects at CRA, Etisalat, Silknet, and TIM, and expansions at Cassava, Deutsche Telekom, Fastweb + Vodafone, Kazakhtelecom, and Orion Telecom.

Nokia is integrating Nemotron and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit into its Autonomous Networks Suite , Cisco has put fine-tuned Nemotron models into Crosswork AI for IP and optical transport operations, and TCS, BT, and NTT DATA are building agents for installation inspection, fault diagnosis, remediation, and early detection of network degradation.

The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture is available now. It pairs Vera Rubin infrastructure for model workloads with Vera CPUs running agent harnesses and the OpenShell runtime, and BlueField DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for out-of-band monitoring and in-silicon policy enforcement. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA.

NVIDIA says Sentry, built on DOCA and running on BlueField-4, quarantines and stops an agent within milliseconds when it tries to move outside its software boundary. The company also claims up to 20 percent higher agent capacity with Sentry, 30x higher throughput per megawatt for agentic workloads on Vera Rubin NVL72, and twice the performance of x86 processors for Vera CPUs, with no comparison configurations or workload conditions given for any of the three.

The architecture runs on Linux and Kubernetes from Canonical, SUSE, and Red Hat, on Windows through Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and on AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, with edge deployments on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, and DGX Station. SAP is integrating OpenShell with the Joule Studio runtime. ServiceNow announced general availability of ServiceNow Arc, with runtime governance through its Super Intelligence Control Tower and enforcement through OpenShell; its AI Passport authority layer extends policies to OpenShell and Sentry and can revoke an agent’s access across software and hardware within seconds.

Dell Technologies, Cisco, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro are building infrastructure on the architecture. CoreWeave, Crusoe, Firebird, Firmus, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Vultr are working on cloud deployments, and 1Password, Check Point, CrowdStrike, Cisco, F5, Fortinet, Microsoft, Okta, Palo Alto Networks, TrendAI, and Zscaler are integrating support into their agent security products.

Volvo Cars is adopting NVIDIA Hyperion and the Alpamayo Stack; Mercedes-Benz is extending its work on the platform to L3 and L4 capabilities; Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is showing its ID. Buzz AD platform on Hyperion, and Einride is building its autonomous freight driver on Hyperion with Halos, Alpamayo, and Cosmos. Bolt has selected the Alpamayo Stack for a European robotaxi program that starts with future Hyperion-based Lucid vehicles, with driving data collection in Madrid in 2027 subject to regulatory approval and a planned rollout of at least 25,000 L4-capable Lucid vehicles.

NVIDIA introduced Halos SAFE, the Safety Assurance Framework for Evaluation, to connect simulation, software- and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, road testing, and fleet monitoring into traceable safety evidence, with dSPACE, IVEX, and TÜV Rheinland as collaborators. Alpamayo 2 Edge is a 2-billion-parameter reasoning model built on Cosmos 3 Edge’s Nemotron-based foundation, optimized for DRIVE AGX Thor and designed to run at 10Hz for in-vehicle scene understanding and motion planning. AlpaJudge scores driving explanations, Foundation4D labels multicamera video without lidar input, and new Cosmos 3 Nano variants add synchronized multiview, multicamera, and lidar generation.

Cosmos Data Factory’s AV blueprint turns driving video and vehicle signals into curated, labeled datasets, and Alpamayo Agentic Factory, due in early 2027, will connect data preparation, post-training, and simulation evaluation. NIM inference containers now cover Alpamayo 1.5 and NuRec Harmonizer. Porsche is leading a Volkswagen Group data workflow on Microsoft Azure through Voxel51, Cosmos Data Factory, and Omniverse NuRec, which Porsche projects will cut repeated physical test drives by up to 90 percent and development-cycle duration by up to 85 percent.

Agile Robots’ Agile ONE SN reference humanoid pairs Isaac GR00T with Jetson Thor and is scheduled for early 2027. The Agile ONE S body stands 1.40 meters, weighs 40 kilograms, and provides 31 degrees of freedom with a 3-kilogram payload per arm; its dual WUJI Hand 2 five-finger hands each offer 20 degrees of freedom, 1kHz force control, and tactile sensing. Onboard Jetson Thor compute delivers a stated 2,070 FP4 teraflops and 128GB of unified memory; sensing comes from head and wrist cameras, lidar, and inertial measurement units; and NVIDIA plans to integrate on-robot safety protocols with Halos.

SimReady Central Library carries more than 2,000 robotics and factory assets, and the Human 1M Dataset holds synchronized three-view video and 3D hand tracking; both are on Hugging Face, with the full Human 1M Dataset open to Cosmos Coalition partners.

Halos, built on IGX Thor, is the safety platform alongside them, with robotics partners integrating or evaluating it for industrial and warehouse use. bodyEvidence: VAST Data announced that DeepL is deploying the VAST AI Operating System as the data foundation for the research environments behind its written and real-time voice translation. Based on current deployment plans, DeepL expects roughly three times the storage capacity of the NVMe hardware it already runs, and it will use VAST’s SyncEngine to migrate data out of its incumbent environment. DeepL’s platform serves more than 200,000 business teams, and the company says real-time voice training is what is driving the new data demand.

The threefold figure covers DeepL’s existing NVMe infrastructure, and DeepL frames the gain as room to scale model development without a corresponding increase in physical hardware. Neither company breaks the gain down between data reduction, erasure coding, and consolidating separate pools onto one platform, and VAST has not tied the figure to Amplify , the program it launched in January with a claim of up to 6x effective capacity from existing SSDs. Drive models, raw capacities, and a deployment timeline were not disclosed.

SyncEngine, the AI OS component that catalogs and migrates data, moves DeepL’s data from the incumbent environment onto the VAST platform. From there, the platform serves file and object storage from one system, which DeepL says simplifies the data structure underneath its research teams and gives it flexibility as the workloads change with the models.

“VAST gives us the performance and reliability we need while allowing us to make significantly more efficient use of the infrastructure we already operate,” said Stefan Andresen, chief scientist at DeepL. “Just as importantly, it gives us a path to make data more easily accessible across our own data centres and, over time, cloud environments, reducing the manual data movement that can get in the way of research.”

DeepL Voice, introduced in November 2024 for live multilingual conversation, is the workload pushing the requirements. Recent updates let it preserve characteristics of a speaker’s voice across languages, and DeepL says training those capabilities puts heavier demands on data access and infrastructure performance than text, with efficient movement between training and production environments as the priority.

The deployment starts in DeepL’s data centers, with plans to extend VAST into cloud environments over time so researchers get the same access to datasets wherever the training cluster sits and stop copying data between sites by hand. Neither company has said which VAST services the cloud phase will use or when it begins.

“As AI moves into production, infrastructure reliability becomes just as important as raw performance,” said Jeff Denworth, co-founder of VAST Data. “Written language, real-time voice and the next generation of AI experiences all place different demands on data, but researchers should not have to redesign the underlying infrastructure every time the model or product changes.”

VAST positions the AI OS as a common data foundation across model development, training, and inference, consolidating file and object services with consistent access across distributed infrastructure. DeepL follows a run of VAST announcements this fall, including DataEnclave for running models on regulated data inside NVIDIA confidential computing and the CrowdStrike integration that went live in September.
