articles.title: Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA Adds a 256-CPU Vera Rack, a Groq 3 LPU Inference Rack, and a 64GB GB10 Desktop
articles.summary: Dell builds its case for the expansion on cost of ownership, citing a September 2026 Signal65 and Futurum Group analysis that puts the Dell AI Factory at up to 90 percent more cost-effective than public cloud over two years, a figure that assumes deskside and data center systems running knowledge, sales, and software development workloads. Dell also cites Goldman Sachs and Gartner projections that agentic AI will drive 24x token consumption while inference costs fall more than 90 percent by 2030. These are vendor and analyst figures, and we did not audit them.
bodyEvidence: Dell Technologies expanded the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA today at NVIDIA GTC Berlin with a 48U PowerEdge M9882 rack holding 256 NVIDIA Vera CPUs for agentic workload execution, the PowerEdge XE9810 rack-scale inference system built on Groq 3 LPUs, an air-cooled two-socket Vera server, a 64GB Dell Pro Precision with GB10, and a set of validated software and deskside deployment templates. The software is available now, and the new hardware arrives between this month and early 2027. Dell says the platform has passed 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter.

Dell builds its case for the expansion on cost of ownership, citing a September 2026 Signal65 and Futurum Group analysis that puts the Dell AI Factory at up to 90 percent more cost-effective than public cloud over two years, a figure that assumes deskside and data center systems running knowledge, sales, and software development workloads. Dell also cites Goldman Sachs and Gartner projections that agentic AI will drive 24x token consumption while inference costs fall more than 90 percent by 2030. These are vendor and analyst figures, and we did not audit them.

“Enterprises used to think about AI infrastructure as an IT budget question, but that’s changed. AI infrastructure is no longer a cost center. It’s a value creation center,” said Michael Dell, chairman and chief executive officer of Dell Technologies.

The Dell PowerEdge M9882 packs 256 NVIDIA Vera CPUs into a single 48U rack as Dell’s build of the NVIDIA Vera CPU Rack , aimed at the CPU side of agentic work: orchestration, tool use, code execution, and evaluation, with model inference left to GPU clusters. Each Vera CPU carries 88 Olympus cores, so a full rack comes to 22,528 cores. NVIDIA’s reference design specifies 400TB of LPDDR5X, 300TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth, and 64 BlueField-4 DPUs per rack; Dell has not yet published the M9882’s memory or networking configuration.

Dell’s argument for a CPU-only rack is power and cooling: separating CPU execution from GPU clusters lets a data center size each pool to its workload, which Dell says makes better use of power and cooling capacity than over-provisioned mixed-use servers. The M9882 is the second CPU-only agentic rack announced this month, after AMD’s Helion blueprint , which packs up to 32,768 EPYC cores in an open OCP design. Dell lists M9882 availability as Q1 CY27.

The Dell PowerEdge R8822 brings Vera to conventional data centers as an air-cooled, two-socket 2U server for standard 19-inch racks. Dell lists agent orchestration, sandboxing, reinforcement learning, and data processing and analytics as target workloads, and the chassis takes up to four double-wide GPUs. It ships this month, which makes it the first of the new PowerEdge platforms to reach customers.

The Dell PowerEdge XE9810 is Dell’s first Groq LPU rack-scale inference system, with 16 direct-liquid-cooled compute trays built on NVIDIA Groq 3 LPUs. Dell positions it as a disaggregated complement to GPU clusters for production agentic AI, with consistent time to first token at scale as the design target. Dell has not published the LPU count per tray, throughput figures, or a full system configuration, and the XE9810 is due in Q1 CY27.

The Dell Modular Data Center with NVIDIA DSX POD is a containerized reference design that ships with compute, storage, networking, rack-level power, and liquid cooling integrated and validated at the factory, so a site connects it to prepared power. Dell says deployment at a prepared site can move from six months to 14 days, and capacity grows by adding containers. It is slated for early 2027.

For telecom operators, NVIDIA Aerial RAN Computer (ARC) platforms on Dell PowerEdge servers run RAN and AI workloads on one compute footprint, which Dell pitches as lower total cost of ownership than separate siloed systems. Dell lists the ARC framework on PowerEdge as coming soon.

Dell Pro Precision with GB10, the system we reviewed as the Dell Pro Max with GB10 , gains a 64GB unified memory configuration on October 23, the same day NVIDIA’s DGX Spark 64GB arrives at $4,999. Dell pitches it at individual developers and small teams running open-weight models locally, and it has not listed a price for the 64GB configuration.

Clustering runs to two 64GB systems or four 128GB systems, and Dell says a customer can start with one system and scale to an eight-node GB10 cluster for more model capacity and concurrent users. We have run eight GB10 systems, two of them Dell’s, against shared storage over 100GbE , where the fleet pulled 24.9GiB/s from one Solidigm QLC array.

Dell Pro Precision with GB300 is coming to Windows with up to 748GB of coherent memory, and 20 petaflops of FP4 compute, which puts the desk-side Grace Blackwell Ultra system inside the Windows environments enterprises already manage. Dell gives no date beyond coming soon.

Dell Deskside Agentic AI Solutions for NVIDIA, the reference deployment templates, are on GitHub now. Five launch blueprints cover agentic coding, agentic VSS, NVIDIA NemoClaw, Hermes Agent on NemoClaw, and a Higher Education AI Lab platform. Each specifies the hardware, models, and software stack for its use case, and Dell says they scale from a single developer to 1,000 or more systems, with support for up to 96 developers on a single platform.

Reflection’s Beam, an Apache 2.0 open-weight model built for software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks, is validated and available on the platform now, as are a knowledge assistant and an agentic AI platform with Mistral. AI observability with Dynatrace and computer vision with Fogsphere follow in Q4 CY26, and SUSE Linux joins the supported operating systems in early Q1 CY27.

Dell’s security architecture for agents stacks three layers: hardware-rooted Dell infrastructure, Red Hat AI Factory software for platform orchestration, and the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture for runtime governance, covering the runtime, network, data, and infrastructure layers. Dell Managed Services for AI, due in Q1 CY27, adds resource optimization, access governance, and consumption and cost management, giving development teams self-service access to AI resources while IT keeps the governance and financial controls.

bodyEvidence: HPE announced updates to HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA today at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, and most of the changes land in HPE Private Cloud AI. Developers, independent software vendors, and AI agents get governed access to the platform’s inference, models, and pipelines through production APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, clusters can now mix NVIDIA H200 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and HPE is introducing the NVIDIA Vera CPU Rack for the agentic workloads that run on CPUs.

HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA bundles models, infrastructure, data, and workflows so enterprises can run AI under centralized security, governance, and operational control. The GTC Berlin updates follow the agentic AI additions HPE made at Discover in June , and they target the same customers: organizations in hybrid, regulated, and sovereign environments that want autonomous AI workloads in production without giving up control of the data and the infrastructure.

“AI agents are becoming an essential part of how enterprises operate and create value,” said Cheri Williams, SVP and GM, Private Cloud and Flex Solutions, HPE. “As organizations deploy AI across industries and increasingly sensitive environments, they need infrastructure that gives them greater control over security, sovereignty, and how enterprise data is accessed and used.”

The new HPE AI Essentials capabilities give developers, ISVs, and AI agents access to Private Cloud AI’s inference, models, knowledge services, and AI pipelines through production-grade APIs and MCP servers, all under centralized identity management and governance. Developers and ISVs can build Private Cloud AI services into applications and industry-specific solutions, and the MCP servers extend the same access to autonomous agents, with versioning and governance scoped by role, tenant, and project. Audit logging records what agents do inside enterprise systems.

OpenAPI is the source of truth for every supported interface, so documentation, software development kits, and code samples are generated from the same definitions. Role-based access control, machine identity support, and audit logging apply to human and agent access alike. HPE also outlined API-first and Kubernetes-assisted onboarding for connected and air-gapped Private Cloud AI deployments, aimed at organizations with regulated or sovereign deployment requirements.

HPE Private Cloud AI now runs NVIDIA H200 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs in the same cluster, so a customer can match each workload to the GPU that fits it under one operating and governance environment. That capability is generally available, as is NVIDIA’s open-source KAI Scheduler, which adds quota-based and priority-based scheduling across projects to improve GPU utilization and workload placement. Our RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition review covers the single-slot member of the same GPU family.

Schneider Electric plans to combine HPE Private Cloud AI with its industrial and operational technology expertise to support what it calls Industrial AI Agents at the Edge, putting inference closer to where operational decisions are made while keeping control over sensitive data. HPE and Schneider Electric have not said which sites or workloads come first.

HPE is introducing the NVIDIA Vera CPU Rack by HPE for the CPU-heavy side of agentic AI and reinforcement learning: agent sandboxes, RL evaluations, and data-processing pipelines that run beside the GPU infrastructure. The liquid-cooled rack carries 256 Vera CPUs and supports more than 22,500 sandboxes. HPE claims 80 percent faster agentic CPU performance without naming a baseline; NVIDIA’s Vera CPU Rack page frames the same figure against traditional CPU infrastructure, also without a test configuration.
NVIDIA’s render of the Vera CPU Rack with a compute tray pulled out

The Private Cloud AI updates, including administrator-enabled developer and ISV access through the HPE AI Essentials API platform, are scheduled to roll out in late 2026. A self-service developer experience covering application and agent registration, API and MCP discovery, and credential management is planned for 2027. Mixed H200 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition clusters and KAI scheduling are generally available now.

articles.title: Valeo and KE:SAI Launch a Franco-German Open-Source Initiative to Build Generalist Autonomous Driving Systems
articles.summary: October 13, 2026 — Paris, France — Valeo, a global leader in automotive technology, and KE:SAI (Kyutai ELLIS Scalable Autonomous Intelligence), the non-profit open science research lab co-founded by kyutai and the ELLIS Institute Tübingen, announce an open-science research collaboration to develop a fully reproducible, generalist AI driving system for autonomous vehicles.
bodyEvidence: Valeo and the open science lab KE:SAI will jointly develop and openly release models, code and weights for autonomous driving research.

October 13, 2026 — Paris, France — Valeo, a global leader in automotive technology, and KE:SAI (Kyutai ELLIS Scalable Autonomous Intelligence), the non-profit open science research lab co-founded by kyutai and the ELLIS Institute Tübingen, announce an open-science research collaboration to develop a fully reproducible, generalist AI driving system for autonomous vehicles.

The program aims to first match, and then push beyond, state-of-the-art performance across all major public driving benchmarks, and to release every component (code, trained models and datasets) as open source to build a strong foundation for democratizing self-driving technology and physical AI. Findings will be shared openly through publications and suppliers and researchers will be able to reproduce the results, build on the model and benchmark their own systems against a common reference.

Marc Vrecko, CEO of Valeo Brain , commented: “This open-science collaboration with KE:SAI marks a strategic milestone for Valeo and the broader European automotive ecosystem. By combining our deep industrial and technological expertise in autonomous driving with world-class open-source research, we are establishing a shared foundation to accelerate the development of physical AI and democratize next-generation self-driving technologies.”

Andreas Geiger, CEO of KE:SAI , commented: “For language models, open source compressed years of progress into months, yet frontier physical AI is still largely closed. Valeo shares our belief that open foundations create more innovation than any closed system ever could. Everything we develop will be open. Every step forward is a step forward for everyone.”

The partnership brings together two of Europe’s leading teams in autonomous driving research, in Paris and Tübingen: valeo.ai, Valeo’s AI research lab, whose open-source models and publications, such as DrivoR and VaVAM, are widely used in the community, and the KE:SAI founding team, known for their open benchmarks and driving stacks such as KITTI, NAVSIM and TransFuser. The partnership’s ambition is to strengthen the European and worldwide automotive ecosystems by giving automakers, suppliers and research labs a built in Europe, open and shared foundation for autonomous driving systems.

Physical AI is widely considered the next frontier of artificial intelligence, but leading efforts, including those in self-driving, remain largely closed with nearly every driving model deployed in the automotive industry proprietary. Automakers and suppliers have no shared, open foundation on which to build, compare and improve autonomous driving systems, leaving them dependent on technology they cannot inspect, adapt or reproduce. At the same time, important research questions regarding efficiency and generalization remain open. Finding out which approaches will make physical AI work reliably at scale requires exploring a wide range of ideas which can’t be pursued by a single lab alone. Developing in the open lets researchers across institutions test, challenge and build on the work. Importantly, building the foundations together, this effort brings academic and industrial research closer together, enabling rapid progress everybody can participate in. This partnership aims to push open source autonomous driving research towards the frontier as we have seen players achieve in the LLM space.

The partnership aims to build one compact AI model that can drive different vehicles, with different sensors, in different environments. The teams will begin by training on large-scale real-world driving recordings, with a model that is designed to transfer across different sensor and camera configurations. From there, the model will go beyond what recorded driving alone can teach. Through reinforcement learning in simulation and learned world models, it will be exposed to rare and safety-critical situations that are scarce or absent in real-world data.

October 7, 2026 – SAN JOSE, Calif. — At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit 2026 (October 12–15), Valeo will present, with OVH Cloud, the validation status of its breakthrough aluminum heat exchanger technology for data center thermal management. This technology is applicable for the rear door cooling modules of rack or fan wall in the core space of data centers (white space). It represents a paradigm shift in the industry.

With over two years of dedicated development in the sector, Valeo is demonstrating its industrial capability and readiness to scale production. Leveraging decades of automotive thermal management, heat exchangers and corrosion know-how, Valeo develops solutions aimed at supporting the AI industry’s exponential scaling needs.

Pascale Herman, Data center & BESS Vice President at Valeo , said: “Presenting our ongoing work at OCP 2026 represents an important step in our journey within the data center ecosystem. Over the past two years, we have made significant progress in evaluating how aluminum liquid cooling can meet the rigorous reliability and performance standards required by modern high-density facilities. By combining these early testing metrics with our decades of automotive thermal management expertise, we are working to develop scalable thermal solutions to support the industry’s evolving infrastructure needs responsibly and effectively.”

As artificial intelligence (AI) workloads push rack densities to new heights, aluminum heat exchangers are being evaluated to provide a powerful, lightweight, more efficient, and scalable alternative to traditional copper hardware. Valeo’s aluminum solutions deliver a 38% increase in cooling capacity and 65% in power density versus traditional copper solutions, while simultaneously reducing fan electrical consumption by 25% . These validation results establish a clear technological breakthrough, directly optimizing Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE) and Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), ideal for retrofitting existing or for new racks.

To evaluate long-term feasibility, and directly address industry concerns regarding aluminum corrosion, Valeo has implemented a comprehensive, accelerated long-run testing framework to simulate long-term reliability and OVH Cloud has been running real time and conditions tests for several months. Testing on Valeo’s specific coating has already successfully reached the equivalent of more than 10-years operating life, fully aligning with the standard infrastructure lifespan of the data center industry. Valeo is currently pushing tests up to 15 years ensuring the material unconditionally meets the stringent, long-term lifespan expectations of data center operators. This ongoing research aims to establish a clear pathway toward production-grade aluminum infrastructure for next-generation data centers.

While the aluminum exchanger takes center stage at OCP 2026, it is part of a broader liquid cooling ecosystem engineered to challenge traditional data center thermal limits and address the industry’s rapid evolution. Valeo’s technology portfolio also includes Direct-to-Chip (DLC) systems (both Single-Phase and Two-Phase) for high-density racks, as well as Zero-Water Immersion Units for Micro-Edge compute applications.

By applying decades of automotive thermal expertise, stringent quality standards, and a vast global manufacturing footprint in all regions, Valeo brings a new industrial perspective to data center cooling. As accelerating AI demand reshapes digital infrastructure, Valeo combines high-volume production scale with cutting-edge innovation to power the digital transition.

articles.title: Valeo Secures Contract for Next-Generation Radar Technology with North American OEM
articles.summary: The new radar technology offers 50 times the resolution of previous generations and enables vital safety features as well as driving and parking functions.
bodyEvidence: Valeo will provide its next-generation corner radar suite—comprising both hardware and embedded software—for the L2+ and L3 systems of a North American electric vehicle manufacturer.
The new radar technology offers 50 times the resolution of previous generations and enables vital safety features as well as driving and parking functions.

The radar platform is built for modularity, allowing the OEM to customize configurations for different levels of autonomy (from entry to Level 3) and supports over-the-air updates for upgrades and future addition of functions such as "Eyes off" capabilities.

June 30, 2026 — Paris, France — Valeo, a global leader in automotive technology, has secured a new contract for advanced safety technologies with a North American electric vehicle manufacturer. Valeo will deploy its corner radar suite, including both hardware and embedded software, for the carmaker’s L2+ and L3 system.

The latest generation of radar is engineered to enable essential life-saving features, including Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB), Lane Keeping Assist (LKA) as well as Safe Exit Protection (SEP). Valeo’s radar system can also support ”Eyes off” functions that could be added over-the-air by the OEM at a later date.

“This landmark win with a major North American automaker validates the unrivaled performance of our next-generation radar in the most demanding environments,” said Marc Vrecko, CEO of Valeo Brain Division . “With 50 times the resolution of the previous generation, this technology fully meets OEM expectations for integration flexibility and low power consumption, while supporting advanced parking features. This new contract is in line with Valeo’s Elevate 2028 growth objectives in the region and supports Valeo’s mission to democratize state-of-the-art safety technology for greater road safety.”

Valeo’s radar platform is designed for maximum modularity. The American OEM will be able to customize the hardware configuration – without increasing hardware complexity – to offer driving and parking functions from entry level to Level 3 of autonomy.
Beyond its technical versatility, the suite is built for global compliance, enabling 5-star NCAP ratings and meeting General Safety Regulation (GSR) requirements.
Finally, the suite supports over-the-air update, ensuring it keeps offering the best performances during the life of the vehicle.

Valeo’s radar family redefines vehicle perception by combining extreme sensitivity with high-performance computing and integrated Artificial Intelligence. Valeo offers both front and corner radars to ensure the reliable detection of small objects over short and long range.

The front radar offers long-range vision capable of detecting hazards at distances of up to 250 meters, ensuring reliable object detection and safe navigation even at high speeds. To ensure peak performance in challenging environments like tunnels or adverse weather, the technology utilizes advanced interference robustness and waveguide antenna technology. Furthermore, the high performance compute architecture supports deep-learning-based fusion, making these vehicles ready for future centralized AI software stacks.

In addition to forward-facing safety, Valeo’s Corner Radar sensors create a protective cocoon around the vehicle. These sensors power critical functions such as Blind Spot Detection, Lane Change Assist, Rear Cross-Traffic Alerts as well as Advanced Parking features ensuring safe autonomous vehicle maneuvering in tight low speed scenarios. By monitoring a vehicle’s blind spots, corner radar sensors significantly enhance driver awareness and safety. During lane-change maneuvers, the system actively assists the driver through visual, acoustic, or haptic alerts and can even facilitate fully automatic lane changes. Additionally, when reversing out of a space, the rear cross-traffic alert system utilizes these sensors to warn the driver of any approaching vehicles.

Leveraging over three decades of industry leadership, Valeo provides best-in-class expertise in radar sensing technology. Our strategic approach prioritizes an optimized architecture that reduces front-end complexity and costs, ensuring we deliver high-end performance.

This 48V eAxle provides a practical solution to the rising emissions costs that will be applied on traditional 4WD. Replacing mechanical components with a more efficient electric drive allows balancing out the extra fuel consumption of the traditional 4×4 systems to meet the strict European standards while remaining affordable.
The 48V 2-Speed eAxle has been selected by Dacia for its new “Hybrid-G 150” powertrain launched on the Dacia Duster, Bigster and in the months to come on the Striker.

This breakthrough technology preserves the iconic 4×4 DNA of the Duster while significantly reducing its CO 2 emissions. The collaboration with Dacia highlights our ability to scale electrification for the mass market and to provide the technology that supports our partners in the transition to sustainable, safe and all-terrain mobility.”

Traditionally, affordable electric axles face a compromise between torque at low speed and high-speed efficiency. This innovation, co-developed by Renault Group and Valeo, resolves this through a new 2-speed architecture:

The 41 kg unit represents the most powerful 48V rear electric powertrain on the market, delivering 31 hp peak. Its compact design allows integration into existing B-segment platforms providing a cost-effective solution to upgrade existing MHEV (Mild Hybrid Electric vehicle) with electric rear-wheel drive function.
